en: (Na0 - 4966) (The Purification Rite named *Ajñānadhvāntadīpikā*) (Author:
Śrī Somanātha)
(Folio No. 38—[Serial] No. (Subject:
Tantra) (The Lamp for the Darkness of Ignorance, 800 Verses)

(On leaf 38 of the *Ṭhākurakaulahāsya*, from the *Ajñātārthadīpikā*): Om. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Having meditated upon the Beloved of Sītā in my heart, I, Somanātha, born of Maheśa, compose the *Bālāvabodha*.
For the sake of understanding, [it is] a lamp for the darkness of ignorance; it bestows success upon those who have mastered the three Mātrikās,
grants mastery over the knowledge of astrology, and provides the happiness of music to physicians who grant success.

Bestower of self-control, giver of peace, remover of poison for those afflicted by poison, and giver of increase to those who possess knowledge of auspicious marks and omens— such is the praise of the treatise.
Without a mantra, no accomplishment arises for embodied beings on this earth;
therefore, for the sake of attaining mastery over mantras here, this manual of mantras (*mantrapaddhati*) is composed.
(4) [It is] unobstructed, consisting of perfected mantras, and providing immediate happiness.

The initiations (*pradāḥ*), renunciations (*saṃnyāsāḥ*), and their practical applications (*saprayogāḥ*) will be explained there in brief. Now follows the definition for examining the teacher and the disciple: one who is of pure lineage, pure conduct, and possesses knowledge.

Devoted to that [goal], belonging to an [appropriate] stage of life, free from anger, knowing the true meaning of all scriptures, enriched with virtuous qualities, born of a noble family, grateful, affectionate toward disciples, and capable of both restraint and favor— (6) [such a person is fit].

One who is devoted to the great mantras of *Heda* and *Kṣoma*, who knows the meaning, exclusion, and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and who is a refuge of pure tradition and compassion— one endowed with such characteristics as these should be a Guru who takes refuge in Hari. (7–8)
Now, the characteristics of the guru and the characteristics of the disciple: the disciple is one who follows the pure path, is illustrious, humble, and pleasant to behold;
he is truthful, devoted to merit, self-controlled in intellect, and free from hypocrisy. (9)
One who possesses characteristics such as being youthful, having all [senses] restrained, and being an abode of compassion—such a person is fit for the authority of initiation;
this concludes the characteristics of a disciple. Now, regarding the commencement of initiation and so forth...

If the initiation for the sake of [attaining] suffering occurs in Caitra, it brings about the fruit together with its presiding deity; in Vaiśākha, it grants all perfections; in Jyeṣṭha, it is said to bestow death;
in Āṣāḍha, it destroys one's kinsmen; and in Śrāvaṇa, it grants prosperity to men.
In Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), it bestows suffering; in Āśvina, there shall be complete success;
in Kārttika, it grants the increase of knowledge; in Mārgaśīrṣa, it is auspicious; in Pauṣa, it destroys knowledge; and in Māgha, it bestows intelligence.

There shall be prosperity in Phālguna, which brings all crops to fruition; initiation is highly commended during either the dark or the bright fortnight. All lunar days are auspicious, provided they are free from the *kuhū* and the *rikta* tithis. (14)
The asterisms Puṣya, Uttara-phalgunī, Rohiṇī, Citrā, Mṛgaśiras, Aśvinī, Śravaṇa, Hasta, Puṣya, Anurādhā, and Jyeṣṭhā are remembered as auspicious for initiation (dīkṣā).
Furthermore, the days of the Sun, Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and likewise the Moon are recommended.
Auspicious yogas, auspicious stars, and auspicious lunar mansions; stable ascendants conjoined with auspicious degrees—these are the times for receiving initiation. Now, [the following]:

The specific [times for practice] are said to be the Mahāṣṭamī or Navamī, the three days beginning with the Dīpamālā festival, during lunar and solar eclipses, on Puṣyārka and Arkarkara days, at the moment of obtaining wealth while asleep, and when given by a woman. These are declared to be the times of accomplishment (siddhakāla).

This is the time for accomplishment (*siddhakāla*). Having worshipped the Guru according to the rules with perfumes, garments, ornaments, and so forth, and having performed the clasping of his feet, one should request the initiation (*dīkṣā*) to be received; then, one should utter the mantra into the right ear.

The Guru should speak three times and perform the rite preceded by the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the procedure prescribed in his own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. This is the rule for the reception of the mantra.
Now, the subsidiary parts of the mantra, as declared by Śiva in the Rurutantra, shall be explained. The mantra...

The best of mantra-knowers, having separately arranged the vowels and consonants in order for both the practitioner and the deity, should count them using the [five] groups beginning with *siddha* and *sādhya*.
He should exclude the *anusvāra*, the *visarga*, the *jihvāmūlīya*, and the *upadhmānīya*.
The wise man should perform the counting of the syllables joined with the *ktvā* suffix and the *tusuṃ* suffix;

[he should also count] the name given by the father or mother, or that which was proclaimed by the Guru (23), as well as those obtained through the recitation of the *saṃhitā*, excluding the *kavala* syllables. *Apa*...

Having discarded any missing syllables, the practitioner should purify the name. (24) A consonant is to be purified by a consonant, and likewise a name ending in a vowel by a vowel; the first [syllable] is to be purified by the first, and the second by the second. (25) a.
In this very manner, all [the letters] are to be purified in due order;
one should count from the beginning that which is the first letter of the name.
This is the sequence for determining the position of the mantra's letters within the Mātṛkā. (26)
One must repeatedly discard the "tuṣka" and "catuṣka" [syllables] again and again,
according to the sequence of the numbers of the accomplished (*siddha*), the unaccomplished (*asādhya*), the self-accomplished (*svasiddha*), and the enemy (*ari*).
When the counting of all mantras has been performed in this manner, (27–28)
One should investigate whether a mantra or a yantra is "siddha" (accomplished), "sādhya" (to be accomplished), and so forth; thus there are these four categories beginning with siddha.
That which is said to be "siddha" along with its mantra is [the first]; the "sādhya" is that which is devoid of the excellence of the twice-born (or the specific qualities of the twice-born). (29)

Excluding the *pu* [group], the remaining three are said to be *susiddha* (well-accomplished). That which is devoid of the *susiddha* is called *yamicchu* (that which one desires); it may be *ādisiddha* (originally accomplished), *asiddha* (unaccomplished), or *madhyasiddha* (intermediately accomplished). *Susiddha*...

That which is established as easily understood and bestowing the fruits of all desires, yet which is difficult to accomplish at the beginning and the end, is achieved only with great hardship. That which is auspicious at the beginning and the end,
and which the enemy might practice against the practitioner, is certainly well-accomplished throughout the three worlds.

(33) Whatever is to be accomplished at the beginning and at the end succeeds only with great difficulty; whatever is an enemy at the beginning and at the end—what should one do that is certain? (34) That which is already established succeeds in its own time.

The *sādhya* [mantra] is mastered through recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*); the *ripu* [mantra], however, kills the practitioner from the very moment it is grasped. (35) Having thus understood the mantra as being *asiddha*, *susiddha*, *siddha*, or *sādhya*, one should [proceed] accordingly.

For the sake of accomplishing what is to be grasped, one should cause [the disciple] to receive the supreme mantra from a scripture or from the mouth of a guru, and then practice it again—either in a city, a town, a village, at the confluence of rivers, or in a forest. (36–37) Upavāsa... (text fragmentary)
At the Netīrtha, the Mahāpīṭha, at the ocean, on the mountain, at the family tree,
at the Siddha-tree, and in the cremation ground; within caves, in houses, at sacred trees, or in the cremation ground— at these sites of the Siddhas, O Śiva.

Having determined the location for the lamp in the field or the house as previously described, one who desires success should write the *kūrma-cakra*, which bestows great accomplishment, and inscribe the eight groups (*aṣṭavarga*) therein;
in the center, however, are the two deities in the directions of Kṣa and Īśāna.
In the nine-square grid of the *pada*-fields, the syllables of the *vargas* are situated in order at the heart, mouth, arms, flanks, feet, and the tip of the tail.
Among those known by the name "Lion" (*dīpa*), these are the lords of the fields: Amṛta and Vṛṣabha.

And likewise Śūlarāja, Vāsuki, as well as Ajagara, Dhūpa, Śakti, and Puras; then Padmayoni, Mahāśaṅkha, Chāyā, and Nakṣatra in succession from the center toward the east and so forth. (42–43) Madhyāt pūrvādi.
Then, the mantra for the worship is to be formulated as follows:
Oṃ hrīṃ amuka-kṣetrapāla, destroy all obstacles! (2) Strike! (2) [Accept] food, liquor, meat, fish, *vaṭaka* cakes, and chewed offerings...
"O you who accept the offering of black beans and cooked rice, eat! Eat! Eat all the wicked ones, including the field-protectors and their retinues! Svāhā!
With this mantra, one should worship all the field-protectors wherever they may be.

The first syllable of the name of a difficult field is its mouth; in the remaining groups, the arrangement of the feet is to be observed. (44) One who is situated in the mouth-position attains success, while one situated in the hand-position enjoys equal prosperity; one situated in the belly-position [attains] wealth.
If it is situated in the tail, one becomes indifferent; if it is in the feet, one incurs suffering.
(45) If it is in the tail, one certainly attains the binding of Mercury while reciting [the mantra];
then, having identified the location of the lamp within the field, the practitioner should become pure. (46)

If even a single initial syllable of the mantras for accomplishing a *kṣetra* is the syllable "Sadhruva," that mantra will be swiftly and perfectly accomplished. (47) Thus ends the illuminators of the mantra-utterances, beginning with "Śrī. Now, the rosary for recitation (*japa-mālā*).
The rosaries for recitation should be made with one hundred and eight, fifty-four, or twenty-seven beads;
they are declared to be of three types—superior, middling, and inferior—in that order. (48)
It is said that [the beads] should be strung with a sacred thread (*brahmagranthi*), joined with Mount Meru, and declared by Śiva;
for the sake of attaining the success of mantras in rites of pacification (*śāntika*) or nourishment (*pauṣṭika*),
they should be strung on a black thread, or else on one made of crystal or pearls.
(50) With which [beads] should one recite for the sake of accomplishing all desires? One should recite with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.
For the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, one should recite with a rosary of lotus seeds. (51) For the goddess Sarasvatī, [a rosary] made of coral; for subjugation, that same [rosary].

It is proclaimed that [the cord] made of ruby or even of silk threads is born from living beings; it should be strung with red threads or even with cloth threads, being white, red, yellow, or black in color. (52)

(53) From the wheel of the six [syllables], for all castes indeed, [there is] the red [color] which bestows everything desired; having tripled the three qualities, one should tie [the thread] according to the treatises on craftsmanship. (54) Each individual [syllable] is a mother-letter (mātṛkā).

The wise man, reciting the four *varṇas*, should take a gem and string it upon a thread, tying a knot between each one. Having tied them with a single knot for each purpose, he should form the *brahma-granthi*.
Then one should begin the refinement of the supreme thread (56);
one should cause the fierce knot of the mantra to be made upon the mantra of the Vidyā,
joining mouth to mouth and tail to tail.
Furthermore, (57) the form of a serpent moving through a garland resembling a cow’s tail is auspicious;
in this way, the best of sages should purify the illusory garland with nine fresh leaves of the *aśvattha* tree. (58) With nine *aśvattha* leaves.

One should fashion it in the shape of a lotus and place the rosary in its center while reciting the root mantra of Mātṛkā. Then, one should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water using the Sadyojāta mantra. (59) Thus.

The Sadyojāta mantra, however, is: "Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; obeisance indeed to Sadyojāta. O Bhava, in every existence, beyond existence, favor me; obeisance to Bhavodbhava. With this mantra, [one should worship] Śiva.

Chanting your mantra (*tavarāram*), one should wash [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*); then, one should worship it with the *Vāmadevya* hymn, using sandalwood, aguru, incense, and other offerings. (60) The *Vāmadeva* mantra is: *oṃ vāmadevāya namo jyeṣṭhāya namaḥ śre*.
Oṃ, salutations to Śarva, salutations to Rudra, salutations to Kāla,
salutations to Kalavikaraṇa, salutations to Balavikaraṇa,
salutations to Balapramathana, salutations to Sarvabhūtadamanaka.
One should smear [the image] one hundred times with sandalwood and other fragrant substances using the mantra: "nāyanamo manonmanāyanamaḥ.
As for the Aghora mantra, it is: "oṃ aghorebhyo 'tha ghorebhyo ghoraghoratarebhyaḥ..."
With the mantra "Salutation to all those of most terrible Rudra-forms," one should fumigate [the deity] one hundred times (100) with incense such as guggulu;
the Tatpuruṣa mantra, however, is: *oṃ tatpuruṣāya*.
With the mantra "vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahī tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt," one should apply sandalwood paste and other substances a hundred times; then follows the Īśāna mantra:

With the mantra: "Oṃ, Īśāna, Lord of all sciences, Sovereign of all beings, the Supreme Brahman, the Overlord of Brahman— may there be eternal auspiciousness, Śiva," one should consecrate Mount Meru one hundred times.

Now, for the mantra of the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā): Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (ṛṣis); the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman Vedas are the meters (chandās); the deity is the power of life (prāṇaśakti) in the form of the glorious [syllable]; and "ĀṂ" is the seed-syllable (bīja).
*Hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), *klīṃ* is the pivot (*kīlaka*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*). Now the mantra:
*Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ laṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ haṃsaḥ sohaṃ*. [The vital breaths] of the deity named [Amuka].
Having first extracted the life-force (*jīva*) from the previous [deity], the life-force of the deity [Amukadevatā] is established here;
having first extracted the life-force, [one extracts] all the sense-faculties (*sarvendriya*) of the deity Amukadevatā: skin, eye, ear, tongue, and nose.
"Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals— along with the twenty-five principles,
come here and remain for a long time in happiness, svāhā! With these three mantras, which are common to all, [one performs] the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).

One should consecrate [the rosary] one hundred and eight times with the mantra: *oṃ māle māle mahāmāle sarvatattvasvarūpiṇī | caturvargastvayi nyastas tasmān me siddhidā bhava*. Then, the rite of fire-offering (*homa*) should be performed.

In order to accomplish the state of the deity, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations and pour the residual drops of clarified butter [into the vessel]. If one lacks the capacity for the fire-offering rites, one should perform double the recitation; therein, by means of the mantra-recitation, the mantra—
One should not cause it to tremble or shake; from trembling, there is loss of accomplishment (*siddhi*), and shaking brings much suffering. If there is sound, disease will arise among people;
falling from the hand causes destruction, and if the thread is broken, death occurs.
Therefore, one should be devoted to diligent effort. Whatever mantra a man recites while remaining unsteady, all of that should be known as fruitless;
the deity becomes angry at that through the application of the thumb of the left hand.

The conjunction of the thumb and middle finger brings about the subjugation (*uccāṭana*) of the illustrious enemy; the conjunction of the thumb and ring finger is certain for the accomplishment of mantras; in the opinion of the wise, the conjunction of the little finger and the thumb is for the rite of eradication (*chedana*);
and the conjunction of the little finger and the thumb is for the recitation (*japa*) for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*).
If the thread becomes worn out, one should knot a new thread and recite the mantra one hundred times.

If it falls from the hand through negligence, one should recite it one hundred and eight times. Having washed the thread once it has been touched by those who have attained perfection (siddhas), one should use it as appropriate.
Now, regarding the procedure for the recitation (*japa*) of the six rites:

one should perform the recitation during the *hemanta* season at the *poṭikā* [time] until sunrise; during the *śiśira* season, one should perform the recitation for two watches (*yāma*) in the first part of the night for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*); and during the *vasanta* season, from after the first watch until midday...
At midday, the rite of attraction (ākarṣaṇa) for the desired object should be performed with mantras; during the third watch of the summer season,
one should recite [the mantra] for the rite of causing hatred (vidveṣa), and then release it until sunset.

One should recite the peaceful mantras at midnight or the end of the night; the auspicious accomplishment of mantras may be performed during any season. For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), it should be done in the forenoon, and at midday for other purposes.

The destruction of affection is performed at dawn; Uccāṭana (driving away) is considered appropriate in the afternoon; Māraṇa (killing) is held to be effective during midday; Śāntika (pacification) is performed at night; and thereafter, all rites may be performed. In the bright fortnight, the second and third [lunar days] are likewise suitable.
The fifth, as well as the third, when conjoined with Mercury, Jupiter, or Venus, is for the purpose of pacification; likewise, the seventh, the sixth, the thirteenth, the fourth, and the ninth,
when conjoined with the Moon, Mercury, or Jupiter, are prescribed for rites of prosperity.
The wise declare that the eighth, ninth, twelfth, and eleventh lunar days,

when joined with Venus or Saturn, are for the performance of the rite of subduing enemies (*dveṣa-karman*). Furthermore, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, Saturday, and the eighth day are for the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*).

This is the sixth [chapter], spoken by Śakra: On the new moon day and the eighth day of the dark fortnight, when that [day] is joined with the asterism of Ṛṣi (Mṛgaśiras) and the Sun (Bhānu), and further conjoined with Saturday (Satabhiṣaj), it kills even one who is protected by Śambhu himself through delusion; therefore, protect yourselves!

Thus, the rites for attaining success [are performed] according to the lunar days and weekdays. Now, the postures (āsana) are described: having ascended to the prescribed posture, one should perform the recitation of the mantra while seated upon a seat made of kuśa grass, deerskin, and cloth, measuring four finger-breadths [in thickness].
One should prepare a very firm, soft, square mat measuring two cubits and spread it over a thread for the sake of attaining success in the yoga-mantra.
With a mind rendered free from fear by the mantra "Hikuṃjaṃbhaṇa hikudivikalīkṛta," one shall achieve the perfection of the mantra.

One does not attain [the goal] thereby; therefore, one should be intent on effort. Tiger skin is for subjugation, while elephant skin is for the accomplishment of the means to liberation. For rites of pacification and nourishment, it should be lotus-seed [skin], and for eradication, buffalo skin.
In the *raṇa* hell, one should sit upon a seat made of human hair for the accomplishment of all rites.

For pacification (*śāntika*), a multicolored woolen blanket is prescribed; for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), a lotus-seat (*padmāsana*) is declared auspicious; for attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), it should be known as the heel-seat (*pārṣṇikāsana*); and for inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), the cock-seat (*kukkuṭāsana*).
For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), one should perform the half-svastika mudrā; for the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), the half-erect posture.

Having worshipped, offered oblations, recited mantras, and meditated upon the deity, one should eat food that is soft, pure, well-cooked, light, and whatever else may be available, while avoiding [forbidden things].
One should eat food that is not corrupted by time, which means avoiding contemptible rice and instead consuming consecrated food;
one who eats in moderation shall attain success (*siddhi*). Otherwise, one should not eat at all, for otherwise a loss of success occurs—all this was spoken by Śiva.
The auspicious accomplishment of mantras follows; now the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of mantras are being written:
birth, life-giving, striking, purification, consecration, piercing, and then nourishment.
This supreme satisfaction, concealment, and protection through these ten mantra-arrangements— having inscribed this excellent Mātrikā-yatra in a vessel of gold or other materials with saffron,
sandalwood paste, or even ashes, O observer of good vows;
Kashmiri saffron is prescribed for the consecration of power (śakti), sandalwood for the Vaiṣṇava fire-ritual, and ashes are declared for the Śaiva rite; furthermore, when writing the Mātṛkā,
the extraction of mantras from within the Mātṛkā is known as "birth" (janana).
Thus is the rite of birth-consecration (*janana-saṃskāra*). Having interspersed the syllables of the mantra with the *praṇava* (OM), the wise one should recite them one hundred times each;
this is declared to be "Jīvana" (the vivifying). They call this [practice] the "Jīvana-mantra."

One who is proficient in the Tantras should perform the *jīvana-saṃskāra* (the rite of infusion of life). Having written the syllables of the mantra, one should strike them with sandalwood water; striking each [syllable] with the seed-syllable of Vāyu (*yaṃ*) is declared to be the *tāḍana-saṃskāra* (the rite of striking). Having written... [the rest of the text follows].
"By the number of syllables in the mantra, one should strike [it] with the letter *repha*; thus is the consecration of awakening (*bodhana-saṃskāra*).

Therein, according to the stated procedure, one should sprinkle this mantra with *aśvattha* sprouts as many times as there are syllables in the mantra, so that all the syllables of the mantra are awakened.

The purification through the two [initiations] is the consecration of empowerment; the mantra-practice of those who contemplate with the mind is performed according to rule at the root and middle of the *suṣumṇā* by means of the light-mantra (*jyotirmantra*).
This is declared by the sages to be the removal and the purification of the three impurities.
With the *trivedibhiḥ* mantra, "Oṃ Hā~," which is the *jyotir-mantra*, this is the purifying (*vimalīkaraṇa*) consecration (*saṃskāra*). Then, with gold, water mixed with *kuśa* grass, or pure water,
one should perform the rite of nourishment (*dāpyāyana-vidhi*) according to the rules using that same mantra.

The consecration by nourishment (*āpyāyana-saṃskāra*) is performed with water using the mantra "Taḥ. The consecration by libation (*tarpaṇa-saṃskāra*) is traditionally taught as the act of offering libations with water while reciting the mantra. The illumination (*dīpana*) of the mantra is said to be the conjunction of the *Tāra* (Om), *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), and *Ramā* (Śrīṃ). This is the illumination.
Refinement (*saṃskāra*) is the concealment and non-disclosure of the mantra being recited. These ten refinements are hidden in all tantras;
by performing them according to the oral tradition (*sampradāya*), the practitioner of mantra attains his desired goal.

"O Goddess, this procedure common to all [mantras] should always be observed. Thus ends the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of mantras. Now, the seven methods (upāyas) of mantras are written here: "If a mantra, even when practiced according to the rule, does not attain success..."

It should be performed again in that same manner; thereafter, the fruit of success will arise. Furthermore, if the mantra does not become perfected from the fist-closure (*muṣṭi*), then the methods spoken of as the seven purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) must be employed therein: liquefaction (*drāvaṇa*), awakening (*bodhana*), and so forth.
By performing subjugation (*vaśya*), pressing (*pīḍana*), drying (*śoṣa*), and burning (*dahana*) in succession through the fire [element],

one will certainly become accomplished (*siddha*). Then, having inscribed the mantra and the yantra upon stone and camphor, one should perform the liquefaction (*drāvaṇa*) and the stringing (*granthana*) of the seed-syllable of Varuṇī according to the sequential method.
One should write [the mantra] joined with the thread upon the chest using saffron;
having written it in the center, one should immerse it in milk, clarified butter, water, and honey.
Through worship, recitation, and fire-oblation, it will certainly grant success once it has been enchanted.
If the perfected one (siddha) has fled, one should cause him to be awakened.
One should recite [the mantra] enclosing it with the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī (*aiṃ*). Thus he becomes awakened and perfected; if not, then bring him under control. This is the awakening.
Having written this mantra on a beautiful birch bark leaf using red sandalwood, kuṣṭha, turmeric, datura, and realgar, it should be worn around the neck;
this is proclaimed as the means for certain success in subjugation (*vaśya*). Thus ends the section on subjugation.
If [the mantra] is not accomplished despite being performed, one should cause it to be oppressed. Having recited the syllables with the *adhara-uttara-yoga*, one should meditate upon the deity;
likewise, one should [meditate upon] the Vidyā as having a red form, beginning with the milk of the *Āditya*.

Having written [the mantra] with the foot of the Sun, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) day after day with that same mantra; one who is afflicted by *alajī* will undoubtedly become successful. Thus ends the section on affliction; even when afflicted, one does not fail to achieve success.
One should cause its drying by means of the two seed-syllables of Vāyu; one should perform the vidarbha-arrangement within the mantra.
This vidyā should be worn around the neck, having been written with the ashes of a banyan tree. Thus is the drying. Even when dried, it is not yet perfected.

If there is the nourishment (*poṣaṇa*) of that which is to be produced, the joining of the seed-syllable of Tripura at the beginning and end of that eternal [mantra]—having written this with cow’s milk on a strip of cloth—one should hold the *vidyā* in one's hand; thus is the nourishment. Even when nourished, [it remains so].
If the fire-seed (vīja) is perfected for the act of burning,
one should join each individual syllable of the mantra— whether at the beginning, the end, the middle, or even half-syllables—
with the fire-seed during the rite of combustion. [One should likewise] recite the mantra with the oil of the *vaṭa* tree...
One should hold [the breath] in the region of the throat; then one becomes a master of mantras, as declared by Śaṅkara.
Thus has the means for all mantras been explained by me.
By this alone one’s purpose is accomplished; what need is there for many?
[Vrata—these mantras consist of seven [chapters], the first two of which are incomplete. Now, the consecration of the wheel (*cakrasaṃskāra*) is being written down. Bhairavī said:
"O Great God, by your grace I have heard this secret of the wheel; now I wish to hear [further]."

Bhairava spoke on the determination of the rite for establishing the sacrificial ground: "Having bathed, the practitioner of mantras should form a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and perform the worship of the Guru. Then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with the Śiva-mantra, [he should place] the Cakra there."

The mantra-practitioner should sprinkle [the vessel] with the *praṇava* (oṃ), thoroughly permeating it; then, having lifted that wheel, he should place it in a golden vessel. He should [offer] the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), milk and so forth, and cool water, along with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar.

One should perform [the worship] in sequence with *rkarā* and the others, with sandalwood, with fragrant substances and the like, with *sthūrī*, and with saffron; thereafter, one should perform the ritual of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) with other incenses.
O Goddess, one should then establish the deities with golden jars.
In the vessel for the debt, [one should recite]: "Oṃ, we know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Yantra;
may that Yantra inspire us. Having drawn the yantra with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, one should consecrate it by reciting this mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing the state of being the deity, one should perform self-purification and worship the six-limbed deity. Having invoked [the deity] there, O Great Goddess,
one should perform the seed-syllable placement (bīja-nyāsa) with the sixteen types of offerings.
Likewise, with hand gestures (*mudrās*) and so forth, one should worship the Goddess there with fruits, betel, and food offerings (*naivedya*).
One should also give a rosary, a sacred thread (*pavitra*), and the like, as well as garments, ornaments, a mirror, a fly-whisk (*cāmara*), and a bell, according to one's means.

Gyaṃ Maheśvarī, one who is intent on their own welfare should bestow all this with effort; then, for the sake of attaining all limited accomplishments, one should indeed recite [the mantra] a thousand times, and thereafter perform the offering of bali and prostrate.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of the *cakrarājaka*, one should pour the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*) [into the vessel].
If one is unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (*homakarman*), one should perform double the number of recitations (*japa*). There, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's means.
In accordance with one's means, having brought a single cow adorned with golden horns and so forth,

and decorated with garments and ornaments— freed from the stinginess of wealth— one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor and the Vedas, and thereafter perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*) of the Goddess.

"O fair-faced one, by the mere satisfaction of the Guru, the accomplishment of the desired goal arises; such is the rule proclaimed in these and other [texts]. [Thus ends the determination of the installation of the yantra in the Śrī Vāmakeśvaratantra. Now, [The text continues: *atha* (now/then).

The determination of the procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhi-nirṇaya*): Thus it is stated in the *Nibandha*: "At an auspicious moment (*muhūrta*), a wise man [should place] a nine-pitcher diagram (*sarvatobhadra*) containing water, honored with perfumes and flowers, provided with cloth, and filled with all medicinal herbs."

Then, having performed the worship of the deity with five types of precious jewels and sprouts, one should again recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Regarding the sprouts, it is said in the Vāsiṣṭha: "The sprouts of the mango, the *aśvattha*, the *vaṭa*, and the *vakula*. Thus it is stated.

The *pañcapallava* (five-leaves) is said by the sages who know the Vedas to consist of the *panasa*, *āmra*, *aśvattha*, *vaṭa*, and *vakula*. Furthermore, the nine gems (*navaratna*) mentioned therein are pearl (*mukta*), ruby (*māṇikya*), lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*), and so forth.

Gomedaka, anudṛd, vidruma (coral), padmarāga (ruby), marakata (emerald), and nīla (sapphire) are used respectively; as it is stated in the Nibandha: "One should seat the well-prepared disciple on the sacrificial altar (vedi) in front of the mouth [of the deity], and [sprinkle him] with consecrated [water]."

One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with the waters of the Śrīṇītīrtha and likewise with the water from the Śaktikumbha, empowered by reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times; "one hundred and eight" means one hundred and eight plus eight, according to the tradition. Then, while accomplishing the mantra...
One should place it on the head, saying "May there be peace (śamastu)," and then offer unbroken grains (akṣatān).
Thereafter, one should worship the Guru. Or else, within that initiation, having worshipped the conch along with the unbroken grains, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with its water eight times.

One should consecrate [the rosary] with the root-mantra of *Raṃ*, and the Guru, placing his hand upon the head of the reciter, should perform the recitation three times. Thus it is stated in the Tantra: "If someone there is unable [to do so], having worshipped that [rosary] along with unbroken rice-grains (*akṣata*), he should consecrate it with its water."
Having placed the root mantra on the eight petals and the *kesara* (filaments), one should mutter it eight times into the ear;
this is the procedure for the oral instruction (*upadeśa*). Thus it is stated in the *Gautamīya Tantra*:
"After the Guru has diligently performed the entire network of ritual placements (*nyāsajāla*) upon his body..."

With a focused mind, one should recite the mantra three times into the right ear; this applies to the twice-born (dvijāti). Thus it is stated in the Tantra: "One should utter the Vidyā three times into the right ear with a single pronunciation. In this manner...
To the left of the twice-born (the Brāhmaṇas) and the women and Śūdras, one should mutter the mantra, complete with its Ṛṣi and other components, into the right ear. Then, O Goddess,
at that very moment, one should mutter the mantra eight hundred times in the presence of Śāradā.

"Having obtained another rare Vidyā, the wise one should recite it eight times, while contemplating with his intellect the excellence of the deity, the guru, and the mantra"— this statement, however, refers to the practice of recitation (*japa*) accompanied by those respective meditations; therein, the guru...

Having prostrated like a staff on the battlefield, he should stand; being addressed with "Arise!", let him act correctly, saying: "May fame, prosperity, beauty, incomparable strength, and health always be yours. Having recited this, he should then rise.
Then, having taken water along with disciples, kuśa grass, and sesame seeds, [he says]:

"For the purpose of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the reception of this such-and-such mantra performed today, this fee (*dakṣiṇā*), consisting of this much gold, whose deity is Agni, [is given] to [the preceptor] of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*), named such-and-such..."
"To you, the Brahmin named Śarman, my guru, I offer this sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). He should dedicate his body, his wealth, and all his vital breaths to him;
from that time forward, he should perform what is pleasing to the guru without any other motive."

When one has received that which is most desired in the world, one should offer it to the guru; this is the rule regarding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the son. One should give the sacrificial fee to the guru as if it were [given] directly to oneself; elsewhere, it is prescribed that one should give all one's possessions.
One should give a cow that has calved for the first time, or one that yields milk, or land that provides a livelihood,
or gold accompanied by clothing, to the Guru; by merely pleasing the Guru, even a corrupt mantra becomes effective, otherwise it does not.

There would be no success; it is not suitable for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*). One should inform the Guru of the collection of materials for receiving initiation (*dīkṣā*). In that interval, one should mutter [the mantra] a hundred times while standing before him, and remain in his presence for three days.
If the Śrī-Śakti does not move [to the disciple], she undoubtedly goes to the Guru; therefore,
one should feed Brāhmaṇas with sweet foods, drinks, and so forth, and together with one's kinsmen, one should eat according to one's capacity, including fish, meat, and other such items.
On the day of initiation, one should feed a married woman who has recently given birth;
regarding the fault of fasting for both the guru and the disciple on that day, it is stated in the *Yoginītantra*: "If the guru, having imparted the mantra, should observe a fast..."
Alas! In the hell of Andhakāra, one becomes a *kumbhīra* (crocodile); it is not otherwise.

Having received initiation, the mantra-practitioner should observe a fast according to the rule. When there is an eclipse of the moon or the sun, the wrathful deity of one's chosen cult (*iṣṭadeva*), having uttered a curse, shall depart to its own abode.

"The mere proclamation of a mantra at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), a field of the perfected ones (*siddhakṣetra*), or in a temple of Śiva is proclaimed as 'instruction' (*upadeśa*). Thus [ends the section] in the *Ajñānadhvaja* composed by the venerable Somanātha Upādhyāya, the son of the venerable Maheśananda.

In the *Nityadīpikā*, the first chapter is titled "The Description of the Purification of Mantras, the Ten Refinements of Mantras, Initiation (*dīkṣā*), and Other Matters. Now follows the exposition of perfected mantras (*siddhamantra*) and so forth; therein, first, the mantra of Gaṇeśa is stated: Oṃ.

The wise know the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati to be the letter at the end of the fifth group (pa) joined with the moon (i). "The end of the fifth" is the letter *ga*; "joined with the moon" means it is accompanied by the *anusvāra*. Thus, *gaṃ* is the single-syllable mantra. By applying this seed-syllable with the six long vowels, one performs the ritual assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

The ritual application (*nyāsa*) and visualization (*kalpanā*) for this venerable mantra: the *gaṇa* is the composer, the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter, and Gaṇapati is the deity. One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the head, face, and heart. The visualization: [one should meditate on] the Lord who is short-statured, with a massive body, and the form of a lordly elephant.

I bow to Gaṇapati, the son of the Mountain’s Daughter, who has a beautiful, pot-bellied form; who is surrounded by bees greedy for the scent of his ichor; whose broad cheeks quiver; who sustains the bodies of his enemies with the darkness of his tusks; and who bears the splendor of vermilion.
Bestowing success and granting desires, and according to another text: "He who shines like vermilion, possessing three eyes,
with broad hips and a large belly, holding in his lotus-like hands a staff, a noose, a goad,
and a beautiful citron fruit shining upon his left shoulder— [he] shone like the rising moon."
Worship Gaṇapati, whose face is like a mass of darkness, whose broad cheeks are full of the flow of ichor, who is adorned like the lord of serpents, and who wears red garments and red unguents;
having thus meditated, one should worship him with mental offerings (mānasopacāra). Then, [the sixteen] offerings...

One should perform worship according to one's capacity; the *puraścaraṇa* for this consists of reciting the mantra ten million times (*lakṣya*). One should then perform the fire-oblation (*havana*) with eight substances and so forth, consisting of one-tenth of that number.
For example: with sweetmeats (*modaka*), flattened rice (*pṛthuka*), parched grain (*lāja*), and roasted barley flour (*saktu*).

One should offer oblations with *bhisokṣupa* stalks, coconuts, pure sesame seeds, well-cooked soups, and plantain fruits; this is the remainder [of the ritual]. Now follows the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati: the seed-syllables of Śrī, Śakti, Smara, Bhū, and Vighna.
First, one should recite: *Oṃ gaṃ gaṇapatim taṃtaṃ varānte vara daṃpadaṃ ukta sarvajanaṃ cānta vaśam ānaya*.
This mantra, consisting of twenty-eight syllables, is proclaimed as the first. *Oṃ śrīṃ*.

*Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ gauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye vara-varada sarvajanaṃ me vaśyam ānaya svāhā*. This is the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati. "Smṛti" (memory) is the letter *ma*, joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*), which is declared to be the seed-syllable of the Earth (*bhū-bīja*). "Smṛti" is the letter *ga*. *Mā*... [text fragment ends].
The *salakāra* (the letter *sa*) joined with the nasal dot (*bindu*) and the vowel *au* results in the syllable *glauṃ*;
thus, *glauṃ* is the mantra. Of this *Śrī Mahāgaṇapati Mantra*, Brahmā is the *ṛṣi*, Gāyatrī is the *chandas*, and Śrī Mahāgaṇapati is the deity.

The seed-syllable is *glauṃ*, the power (*śakti*) is *svāhā*, and the peg (*kīlaka*) is *gūṃ*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation during recitation. One should fashion all the seed-syllables beginning with the six, endowed with the long vowels, as the nine-jeweled meditation (*dhyāna*).
If one were to remember that island in the ocean of milk, it extends as far as the horizon,
frequented by gentle breezes, crowded with celestial trees such as the Mandāra and Pārijāta and their creepers,
and its ground reddened by streams of divine jewels.
One should meditate upon its floor, which illuminates the horizons with the rising sun and moon;
in its center is the Pārijāta tree made of fresh jewels, which constantly increases joy by being perpetually graced by the six seasons; and beneath it...

One should meditate upon Mahāgaṇapati in the great sacred seat (*mahāpīṭha*) within the lotus of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkā*), situated within a triangle that is itself contained within a hexagon; he is to be visualized as having the face of a lordly elephant,
embraced by his beloved who holds a lotus in her hand, and is ablaze with light.

Adorned with the letter *la*, he is the cause of the creation, destruction, and maintenance of the universe, the remover of obstacles, and the bestower of extraordinary goals. Now, for the worship diagram (*pūjā-yantra*): one should then draw a triangle, a hexagon, and an eight-petaled lotus, followed by four spokes.
Now, the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) as proclaimed in the *Yuktayantropaniṣad* is as follows:
one should perform four hundred and forty-four thousand recitations (*japa*),
and then perform the fire-oblation (*havana*) and other rites with the eight substances and so forth, using one-tenth of that number.
Then, one should state the power (*śakti*) "Ṭha," one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*), and Mahāgaṇapati; this twelve-syllable mantra, known as the "bride" (*vadhū*) and containing fire (*agni*), is:
*Hrīṃ Gaṃ Hrīṃ Mahāgaṇapataye Svāhā*. *Hrīṃ* is the heart (*hṛdaya*).
*Gaṃ* on the head, *hrīṃ* on the crest, *mahāgaṇapataye* once on the speech, *svāhā* on the three eyes; having recited the entire mantra with *astrāya phaṭ* [on the weapon], the visualization:
[one should meditate upon him] as pearl-white, with the face of an intoxicated elephant, and [marked by] the moon...
I worship the Lord who has a topknot and three eyes, who holds in his hands a lotus,
a goad, a jewel-pitcher, and a mass of weapons shining like the breasts of the Goddess seated on his lap; and whose hand is placed upon the source of the Goddess’s wealth, which is like a jewel.
One should worship his crown, which is a yantra for his worship, just like the yantra of Mahāgaṇapati.

His preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations (japa); one should perform the fire-oblation (havana) and other rites with a tenth part of that number using Madhūka flowers soaked in the three sweets (trimadhura).

The *gaṇakṛṣi* [mantra] has the *gāyatrī* meter; its presiding deity is Śrī, and its specific deity is Gaṇeśa. One's own seed-syllable (*bīja*), conjoined with the other Śaktis, followed by "vaśyaṃ ānaya" and the two *ṭha*s (ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ), preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ)—this is declared to be the *rudrasaṃkhyākṣara* (eleven-syllabled) mantra.

Then: *oṃ hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ vaśam ānaya svāhā*. For this [mantra], all rites such as worship and so forth should be performed as previously described. First with one [syllable], then with three, then with two, and finally with the whole; this is considered the method for invoking the weapon (*astra*).
One should place [the seed-syllables] on the thumb, the fingers, and the heart and other limbs.

Now follows the meditation: [one should meditate upon the Lord] holding a sugarcane bow in his right hand, with a noose and a goad resting upon his lotus-like hand, and [embracing] the beautiful-limbed woman who stands beside him.
I constantly meditate upon the Lord, who is excessively fond of enjoyment, who is embraced by the dark-limbed Goddess holding a lotus with her hand that touches the tip of his banner,
and who is the three-eyed one with the crescent moon on his crest, his face red from wine and possessing the form of an elephant;
this is his preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*).
The recitation (*japa*) is three hundred thousand times; the fire-oblation (*homa*) consists of ten parts of sacrificial cakes mixed with clarified butter.
Now, the mantra of Heramba: the syllable *ga* with a nasal dot (*bindu*), preceded by the *praṇava* and followed by *namaḥ*, bestows the fruit of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*).

The mantra is *oṃ gūṃ namaḥ*. For this venerable mantra, Gaṇaka is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Hara is the deity (*devatā*), the syllable *ga* is the seed (*bīja*), and Vidu is the power (*śakti*). Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of desired success during recitation (*japa*).
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the six long-consonant forms of the letter *Na*. Then, for the meditation:

one should contemplate the Lord who has the moon as his crest-jewel, whose vehicle is the lion, who possesses three eyes, and whose complexion is smooth like pearls, gold, sapphire, and jasmine; he is the Lord of the Sun.

I worship him who holds a heated mace, a goad, a trident, and a skull-staff—each bearing a severed head, an eye, a skull, and a skull-cup—in his hands; he is self-controlled, fearless, and a bestower of joy.
His worship-yantra is as before; this is his *puraścaraṇa*.

One should perform the recitation (*japa*) three hundred thousand times, and then offer oblations (*homa*) such as sesame seeds soaked in the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*) for one-tenth of that number. Thus it is stated in the *Nibandha*:
"For the propitiation of Saṃvartaka, who stands upon the seat of Brahmā with eyes like nooses... [Hṛdaya].

The mantra, enriched with its own seed-syllable, consists of ten syllables: *Oṃ gaṃ kṣiprasādanāya namaḥ*. Of this venerable mantra, Gaṇaka is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chandas*), and the swift-granting Gaṇeśa is the deity (*devatā*).
One should perform the placement of the hand-gestures (*mudrās*) as described for Kākṣarava. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is as follows:

the elephant-headed one is red, has three eyes, wears a crown of young trees, and holds in his trunk a *bījapūra* fruit containing the seed-syllable, while bearing a noose, a goad, and a wish-fulfilling creeper (*kalpalatā*).
For the *puraścaraṇa* of this [deity] beginning with "Mukhovatāntaḥ," one should perform a recitation (*japa*) of one hundred thousand (*lakṣa*).

At the place of recitation, one should offer ten thousand (*ayuta*) oblations of sesame seeds, or else with the three sweets (*madhuratri-taya*), or with the eight substances prescribed. Now, regarding the turmeric...
The *ṇeśa* mantra consists of five syllables, is established upon the earth (*la*), and has the moon (*u*) as its crest;
it is a single-syllable great mantra that bestows the fruits of all desires.
One should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*) and so forth using the seed-syllable (*bīja*) endowed with the six long vowels.

With the mantra *Śrī Glauṃ*, one should meditate upon the deity Gaṇeśa as having the luster of turmeric, four arms, wearing beautiful garments, holding a noose and a goad, and possessing charming teeth; having thus meditated,
one should perform all the rites of worship and so forth for the Single-Syllable Gaṇapati.
For this [deity], the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of four hundred thousand recitations (*japa*).

One should perform the fire-oblation (*havana*) and other rites with one-tenth that number using sesame seeds mixed with turmeric powder and the three sweets (*trimadhura*). Alternatively, there is the *Vakratuṇḍa* mantra.

The armor of Vakratuṇḍa is long, consisting of six syllables: *vakratuṇḍāya*. Following that, there is an eight-syllable mantra ending with *māyā*: *vakratuṇḍāya māyāntaḥ*. Here, by the word *māyā*, the *kūrca* (the seed-syllable *huṃ*) is to be understood. Thus: *vakratuṇḍāya huṃ*; *vakratuṇḍāya hrīṃ namaḥ*.

Thus ends the second [section]. For this Śrī Vakratuṇḍa mantra: Bhārgava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Vakratuṇḍa is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of my complete success in the recitation (japa) of the six-syllabled [mantra] dedicated to Gaṇapati.
The wise practitioner should perform the six ancillary rites (ṣaḍaṅga). Then follows the meditation:
[one should meditate on the deity] whose color is his own, who has a serpent as a sacred thread, a protruding belly, and a pot-bellied form;
who possesses a single tusk, and who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a noose and a goad.

I take refuge in the auspicious Vakratuṇḍa, the ornament of the three worlds, who is joined with the pair of women through his conduct, whose self consists of six syllables, who is the sole destroyer of obstacles, the wish-fulfilling tree, and who grants swift success even in the Kali age.

Having meditated thus, one should mutter [the mantra]. Having drawn an image of one's enemy on the ground, one should set it ablaze in the region of the fire’s belly and offer a thousand oblations of white mustard seeds and *rājika* (black mustard).
One shall slay the enemies within seven days. [One should worship] Gaṇeśa, who is wrathful and firm.

Having seized the black-colored enemy with one's own *puṣkara* (hand), one should cast him into the fire as if he were the *vaḍavāmukha* (submarine fire). Meditating thus upon oneself with single-minded devotion, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times for three days; thereby one shall expel even Śakra and Śukra.
For this [mantra], the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of twelve thousand recitations (*japa*).

As it is stated in another Tantra: "In the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), killing (*māraṇa*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), pacification (*śāntika*), delusion (*mohana*), and paralysis (*stambhana*)," [the mantra is employed].

The six-syllable mantra of the King (Rājā-Ṣaḍakṣara) undoubtedly brings success in all other undertakings. By reciting it with the word "phaṭ" at the end during the fourth lunar days of both fortnights, one obtains a hundred vessels of food for a year; thus it has been declared.
Having received the great mantra from the guru, being composed, devoted to celibacy,
peaceful, truthful, and a worshiper of the guru— practicing celibacy, self-controlled,
and with a pure and well-restrained mind— one should then recite it ten thousand times.

One should perform the *puruścaraṇa* on a Tuesday morning, or on the fourth lunar day (*caturthī*), being well-composed; one should then undertake its commencement, after which one will certainly attain success. Now, [follows] the *mālā-mantra* of Haridrā-Gaṇeśa.
The Ṛṣi is I myself; the metre is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is Śrī Hari accompanied by Gaṇapati;
[this mantra is employed] for the purpose of enchanting all the worlds, for binding the mouths of all wicked ones, and for paralyzing the movement of evil-living beings.
The application for the recitation (*japa*) follows. Now, the mantra: *Oṃ hūṃ gaṃ gūṃ glauṃ haridrā-gaṇapataye vara-varada sarva-jana-hṛdaya-stambhaya stambhaya svāhā*.
This is the *mālā-mantra*. Now, the six-limbed (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*) ritual: *Oṃ hūṃ geṃ gūṃ glauṃ* [to the] heart.

*Yanamaḥ* to Haridrā-Gaṇapati, *svāhā* to the head; *vaṣaṭ* to the crest (*śikhā*) of the bestower of boons; *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*) that captivates the hearts of all people; *vauṣaṭ svāhā* to the three-pronged weapon (*astra*) for paralyzing; *phaṭ* to the missile (*astra*). [Meditation...]

[He meditates on] that three-eyed, heroic god with an elephant’s face, standing in the center of a red maṇḍala upon a jeweled lion-throne, radiant with yellow-colored garments, unguents, garlands, and ornaments, and holding a noose and a goad in his hands.
With one-pointed mind, one should meditate upon the God, the Lord of the Goddesses, who holds a drum, an axe, and bestows fearlessness and boons; then, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight,
one should perform the oblation ten times that amount, and thereafter, O auspicious lady, one may perform the ritual activities.
For the attainment of results, there is a preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consisting of twelve thousand recitations of this [mantra].
Next is the mantra of Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati; it is stated in the *Tantrāntara*:
"First, having uttered the *praṇava*, then the seed-syllable of Śambhu, and after that, Hari..."

One should visualize the letter *da* mounted upon the light-stable (*sthitaprabhā*) vowel *u*; this is the hero (*śūra*) residing in the right eye, proclaimed as the fourth *vāja*. The two subsequent letters, *gha* and *na*, possess the luster of a bull and are joined with the two *puṣṭī*s in the third heaven.

The seed-syllable of the Lord of Devas (Hrīṃ) followed by the letter 'e', then having extracted Durgā (Druṃ), one should utter the eight syllables; with the wife of Vaiśvānara (Svāhā) added, this is proclaimed as the fifteen-syllabled mantra. Some say this mantra begins with the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa (Gauṃ).
They declare this to be the mantra: *Oṃ hastipiśāci likhe svāhā*.
This is the extraction of the mantra. Likewise, neither a specific lunar day (*tithi*), nor a constellation (*nakṣatra*), nor fasting is prescribed;
the mantra bestows the fruit of all desires through practice according to one's own will.

The wise practitioner, performing the meditation as prescribed by the venerable Gurus, should recite the single mantra three times for each of the [categories] beginning with *asiddha*. He should meditate upon Gaṇeśa as having a red form,
adorned with red ornaments, wearing red garments, possessing three eyes, and seated upon a red lotus throne.
He stands with four arms and a massive body, possessing two fangs and a smiling face;
in his left hand he holds a bowl of modaka sweets, while from his mouth hangs a long, dangling tusk which he supports with his right hand; and in his other [right] hands he holds a noose and a goad.

One should worship [the deity] who is encircled by a mass of matted locks, adorned with the crescent moon on his forehead, decorated with all ornaments, eternally present, and never impure from eating leftovers;
even one who has not rinsed his mouth may worship him. This is the mantra of the venerable Ucchiṣṭagaṇapati.

For this [mantra], the sage is Sūryasugrīva, the meter is Trivṛt Gāyatrī, and the deity is Ucchiṣṭagaṇeśa; one should perform the visualization (nyāsa) using the seed-syllable beginning with the letter *ga*.
Its preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), followed by its tenth part [in oblations].
One should perform the oblation and other rites with *tila* and mustard seeds soaked in honey and clarified butter.
Beginning from the fourth day of the dark fortnight until the fourth day of the bright fortnight,
one should daily recite the *Śrīsūkta* a thousand times according to the rules of the *Poṣadha* vow, and one should bathe [the deity].
I, Gaṇeśa, who am ever beloved by Haṃsa, having fashioned an image [of myself] out of white Arka wood or red sandalwood, measuring only the size of a thumb,
and having installed it in the presence of the fire of wisdom and my Guru, I shall recite [the mantra] six thousand times.

The mantra for this [deity] shall certainly be: *Oṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Laṃbodara Hastimukhāya Ucchiṣṭāya Mahātmane Krauṃ Kraiṃ Hrīṃ Ucchiṣṭāya Svāhā*. One should prepare his yantra as an eight-petalled lotus consisting of four gates.
The causal mantra is: *Āṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ gaṃ hastimukhāya lambodarāya sarvaphalaprādāya mahātmane ucchiṣṭāya oṃ krauṃ śrīṃ kheṃ kheṃ ucchiṣṭāya svāhā oṃ hastimukhāya lambodarāya*.

To this Ucchiṣṭa Mahātman, Āṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Gaṃ, to the Elephant-faced One who bestows the fruit of all desires, to the Ucchiṣṭa, Svāhā! There is a specific rule for the six-limb assignment (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa):
Hrīṃ Oṃ, to the Elephant-faced One, to the heart.
Namaḥ to Lambodara, Śirase svāhā; Oṃ to Uchiṣṭa, Śikhāyai vaṣaṭ; Mahātmane Kavacāya huṃ; Āṃ Krīṃ to Netrāya vauṣaṭ; Oṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Gaṃ to Uchiṣṭāya svāhā. A.
Strāyaphaṭ! He whose belly hangs down, holding a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows;

who has the face of an elephant; whose body is red as vermilion; who is naked; who is intent upon the mouth of a woman; who is greedy for the taste of a woman's vulva; and who is deluded by passion—[worship] him.
The practice consists of being intent on a firm embrace of the left lap of the noble ones, [offering] one’s own lotus-feet which grant desired fruits;
this should be performed daily, beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.

One should recite the mantra ten thousand times for the sake of its accomplishment; once accomplished, one's own mantra becomes capable of performing all rites. One should perform libations (*tarpaṇa*), consecrations (*abhiṣeka*), and fire-offerings (*homa*) in the tenth part [of the recitation]; every day, one should [recite] the mantra with *tṛṇa* grass.
One should worship the Lord of Ganas with various foods, edibles, and offerings resembling nectar; having thus satisfied them, the mantra will certainly become perfected.
On the day of the Pushya asterism or on a Sunday, the Mula mantra arrives.
At the time of the ritual union, one should fashion an image of Vaināyaka from *niṃba* wood the size of a thumb, adorned with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Whomever one contemplates in the mind, one should place that person in the midst of the syllables of the mantra.

"Reciting 'Draw each one [toward me],' one should chant [the mantra] one thousand times, or one hundred and eight times, by the grace of the Lord of the Gaṇas. Thus ends the ritual manual for the Ucchiṣṭa-Gaṇapati mantra. Now, there is another [method] in another tradition.
Now, for the *mālā-mantra* of Ucchiṣṭagaṇeśa: *oṃ hrīṃ ekadantāya hastimukhāya lambodarāya sarvapāpapraśamanakārakāya sarvavighnādhipataye sarvārthasiddhidāyakāya*.

O Bestower of Wisdom, who pacifies all suffering, come, come, O Blessed One! Bring all people under my control; paralyze the faces of wicked people, delude them, and summon them—do not let my enemies [prevail].

*Raya* (2), *uccāṭaya* (2), *ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. Oṃ āṃ krauṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ gauṃ gūṃ glauṃ gaṃ! To Gaṇapati, the bestower of boons, bring all people under my control; *ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā*. I shall declare the extraction of this mantra; listen, O Kama.

Having extracted the *pacāntaka* (the letter *pa*) from the *lānana* (the *la*-group), one should extract the seed-syllable of Indra (*i*), enriched by the fourteenth vowel (*au*) and adorned with a *bindu* on its head. This single-syllabled Great Vidyā was proclaimed by the Lotus-born One (*Padmayoni*). Regarding its ritual of worship...

Having performed the previously described rites for the Great Gaṇapati, such as the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*), and having prepared the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the sages (*ṛṣi*) and so forth.
Then, one should perform the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) there with one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*) preceded by the six long vowels. Its variations are as follows:
O Goddess, one should recite the *Tārā* mantra beginning with *Lakṣmī*, or that beginning with *Kūrca*,
or that beginning with *Japa*; likewise,
one should recite the *Vidyā* beginning with *Kāma*, or the *Vāgbhava*, which is like another *Kāmadhenu*, consisting of six syllables.

O Beloved, this Great Vidyā consists of four seed-syllables and is joined with the weapon-mantra of Mahāvidyā-rakṣarī; it is the sovereign of the Vidyā-vajrī-jāyā. This Great Vidyā is extremely difficult to obtain in the three worlds and is the direct bestower of the four aims of human existence.
The destruction of sins for these [mantras] is achieved through renunciation (saṃnyāsa), worship, preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa), and so forth; all such work belongs to the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati.
Thus ends the *Mañjarī* composed by the venerable Somanātha, the Upādhyāya of Maheśa.
In the *Nadhvāntadīpikā*, the second chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Gaṇapati Mantra," is concluded. Now, the Bhairava mantras:
*oṃ namaḥ śivāya* is the six-syllabled mantra; *oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ*; *oṃ namaḥ śivā*.

*Oṃ hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ oṃ namaḥ śivāya oṃ jūṃ saḥ*—this is the *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra. *Oṃ hrīṃ ṭhaḥ*—this is the *Nīlakaṇṭha* mantra, which removes the two types of poison. *Myaiḥ*—this is the *Cintāmaṇi* mantra. *Dasyeṃ*—this is the mantra.
Oṃ hrīṃ! Salutations to you, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who dwells at the foot of the banyan tree; salutations to Rudra, the consort of Śambhu, whose limbs are solely intent on meditation. Oṃ hrīṃ!
Salutations to the Blessed One, Dakṣiṇāmūrti; grant me wisdom.
Svāhā! Oṃ auṃ, salutation to the heart; Oṃ raṃ, to the head; Oṃ juṃ, to the crest-lock; Aiṃ, to the armor; Āṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes; Aḥ, phaṭ to the weapon.
Of this Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra, Caturmukha is the seer (ṛṣi).
The Devī-gāyatrī is the meter; Dakṣiṇā-Sadāśiva is the deity;

the application is in the recitation for the sake of attaining success in the mantra. Alternatively, the arrangement of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) may be performed using the words originating from the mantra. The visualization (dhyāna): [one should meditate upon] the great, lofty shade of the banyan tree, [and] the ruby-colored...

One should meditate upon the Lord, the Leader of the World, seated at its base— [the tree] which is radiant with blossoms, adorned with variegated leaves made of emeralds, and decorated with great ornaments of the nine jewels shimmering like waves; [and the Lord] engaged in exposition.
Holding her left foot with arms adorned with garlands of grapes and lotuses,
she rests upon a golden yogic seat in the center of the moon, which is marked by the syllable *Oṃ* and situated within the lotus of the Upaniṣads.

May Śiva— three-eyed, moon-crested, with a vast radiance like the luster of milk, and possessing pure intellect— protect us; may he whose hands hold a crystal rosary, silver-colored pearls, a jar of nectar, and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) grant us well-being.
I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who holds a mallet in his uplifted hand, whose crest is the moon, who possesses three eyes, and who is adorned with various ornaments; for this [mantra],
the preliminary recitation consists of one hundred thousand repetitions, followed by ten-thousandth parts of that number of offerings of lotuses with ghee.

One should perform the oblation (*havana*) with the Aghora mantra: *hrīṃ sphura (2) ghora (2) tarāghora sa-vṛṃca-ṭhaka-ha-dama (2) bandhva (2) ghātaya (2) pātaya (2) hūṃ phaṭ aḥ*. Then [the mantra]: *oṃ klīṃ ṣu hūṃ phaṭ hauṃ*.

This is the mantra consisting of a single syllable (*ekākṣaramantra*). Its preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of reciting it five hundred thousand times (*pañcalakṣyajapa*). One should then perform the fire oblation (*homa*) and other rites with *karavīra* flowers, numbering one-tenth of that amount.
Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *paṅkti* meter (*chandaḥ*), and Sadāśiva is the deity (*devatā*).
*Tā hoṃ hīṃ hūṃ haiṃ haḥ*—this is the six-limbed *Śiva-mantra*. Now follows the eight *Bhairava-mantras*. Now their names: Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava, Vaṭuka, and Bhūtanātha.

The withdrawal [mantra] and the eight Bhairavas: *oṃ kṣauṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ* is the mantra of Kṣetrapāla. *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ hrauṃ hrauḥ hraḥ hana (2) svāhā* is the Saṃhāra mantra. *oṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ hūṃ hrauṃ hraḥ*.
*Svāhā oṃ hrīṃ bhūtabhairavāya namaḥ svāhā*—this is the mantra of Bhūtabhairava.
*Oṃ namaḥ paśupataye*. Now, the mantra of Khaṅgarāvaṇa: *Oṃ bhūtā...*
Salutation to the Lord Rudra, who possesses a dancing sword, whose roar is like that of Rāvaṇa, who dances, whose body is smeared with ashes from the cremation ground,
who wears a garland of bells and skulls, and who is clothed in a tiger skin.

O you who have made the moon of fame your crest-jewel and the black serpent your sacred thread; O protector of the world, who turns back the hosts of Vala; O destroyer of the entrails of all beings; O Kaṭa; O Rudra, pacify [the affliction] with your goad! Prave... [The text is incomplete.]
Śaya (2) āveśaya (2) Caṇḍāsidhārapataye Rudrāpayati Svāhā—this is the mantra of Khaḍgarāvaṇa. Oṃ Bhūtādipataye Svāhā.
Oṃ Hīṃ Vaṭukāya Āpamuddhāraṇāya Kuru (2) Vaṭukāya Hrīṃ.

Thus ends the mantra of Vaṭukabhairava. Thus concludes the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Śiva-mantras," in the *Jñānadhvāntadīpikā* composed by the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrī Maheśabhaṭṭa Śrutasomanātha.

Now, the mantra of Bhuvanīśvarī: the syllable *ra* (Rakulīśa) mounted upon fire (*agni*), followed by the eye (*vāmanetra*) and the moon (*candravat*). This is declared to be the single-syllabled Vidyā, Bhuvanatāriṇī.
Of this venerable Bhuvaneśvarī mantra, Brahmā is [the seer].
The Seer is [...................................], the Power is Hāṃ, and the Application is for the sake of attaining my desired goal during the recitation.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable of Lajjā (*hrīṃ*) conjoined with the six long vowels. [Now follows] the meditation (*dhyāna*).
Śrī. Oṃ! [I bow] to her whose luster is equal to the rising sun, who has surpassed the fresh *japā* flower, who is adorned with a crescent moon;
she who shines with three eyes and a crown, who possesses earrings sparkling with various gems and rubies, and who is radiant with necklaces, armlets, girdles, and clusters of jewels.

"I bow to Ambikā, who is adorned with various colorful garments and whose lotus-like hands hold the noose, goad, *iṣṭa* (boon), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*). Having thus meditated, one should recite:
*Aiṃ Tripurā Bhuvaneśvarī Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*. Of this [mantra] of the venerable Bhuvanī...
For the Śvarī-mantra: Brahmā is the ṛṣi, Triṣṭubh is the meter, Śrī-Bhuvanīśvarī is the deity, Hrīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hrīṃ-Śrīṃ is the power (śakti), Aiṃ is the pin (kīlaka);
its application (viniyoga) is in this recitation for the sake of attaining my desired goal. Here too...
The six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) is performed with the *jāpya* seed-syllable; the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as before.
Thus is Māyā Bhuvanīśvarī. *Āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ* is the mantra for Pāśādi-Bhuvanīśvarī.
*Oṃ hrīṃ heṃ ūkṣe chaikṣaḥ strīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ* is the mantra of Tvaritā.

Now, the mantra for Aparāpatrakaṇṭhakī-viśvā: *oṃ kṣyeṃ strīṃ gleṃ oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ nityaklinne madadrave aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ svāhā*. This is the fifteen-syllable great mantra (*pañcadaśākṣarī-mahāmantra*). Also: *oṃ nityaklinne madadrave svāhā*.

Thus is the twelve-syllable mantra: *hrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ krauṃ nityamadadrave svāhā*. This is the second Tripurā mantra. *Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*. Now, the mantra for the one mounted on a horse: *oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krīṃ ehyehi parameśvari svāhā*.
Oṃ hrīṃ ehi parameśvari svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ padmāvatī svāhā | This is the mantra of Bhuvaneśvarī. Now, the mantra of Durgā: Oṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai namaḥ svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ mahiṣamardinīṃ svāhā | Oṃ...

Durgerakṣiṇī svāhā! Oṃ durgarakṣiṇī svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ, to you who are garlanded with flames and surrounded by a host of vultures, svāhā! Oṃ jvala jvala, O wielder of the trident, [subdue] the wicked grahas, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Oṃ śūlini!

"O you who subdue evil planets! Svāhā! Arise, O Puruṣikī! Why do you sleep? A danger has arrived; whether it be possible or impossible, pacify it for me, svāhā!"—this is the mantra of Durgā dwelling in the Vindhya mountains.
Now, the fourteen-syllable mantra of Sarasvatī: *Oṃ Traḥ*.

This fourteen-syllable Vāgvādinī mantra has Kaśyapa as the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ as the meter (*chandaḥ*), the fourteen-syllable Vāgvādinī as the deity (*devatā*), *Vaṃ* as the seed syllable (*bīja*), and *Svāhā* as the power (*śakti*).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for recitation (*japa*) for the purpose of attaining knowledge (*vidyā*). *Vaṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ*; *oṃ daṃ* to the head; *vaṃ* to the crest (*śikhā*); *daiṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*); *vāgvādinī* to the eyes; *svāhā* to the weapon (*astra*). Meditation (*dhyāna*): [as follows].
May she—whose lotus-like hands are raised with an inkwell, a pen, and a book;
who is as white as a jasmine, a mandāra flower, and a full-blown lotus; and whose crest-jewel shines with a crescent moon—be the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence.
*Ginībhāratīvaḥ oṃ vadavada vāgvādini svāhā*.
Now, another mantra: *namo bhagavati vāgvādini svāhā*. And another: *oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*.
And another: Omitting the corrupt syllables *ai vā caspa te praṃmlaḥ laḥ oṃ*, [the mantra is] *śrī asya śrī ṣoḍaśākṣarī vāgvādini*.
For this mantra of sixteen syllables, Kaśyapa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and the deity is the auspicious sixteen-syllabled Vāgvādinī.
The deity is Nīdevatā; the seed-syllable is Aiṃ; the power (śakti) is Svāhā; the pin (kīlaka) is Krīṃ Krīṃ;
the application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining success in speech during recitation. Oṃ Aiṃ [is] the heart; Namaḥ [is] the head;
Bhagavatyai [is] the crest-lock (śikhā); Vada vada kavaca [is] the armor.

"Vāgvādinī netrā svāhā astrā"—thus are the six limbs [of the ritual]. As for the visualization (dhyāna): she is white, adorned with unguents, garlands, and garments, radiant with a crescent moon, and holding a book, a rosary, and a vessel filled with *svadhā* offerings.
I bow to the goddess of speech, who holds a lute and a lotus in her lotus-like hands, who sits upon a lotus, whose breasts are slightly bent, who possesses a beautiful smile,
who bestows the power of eloquence, who has three eyes, and who grants the wealth of good fortune.
The reciter: *Oṃ namo bhagavati vāgvādini svāhā*.
Now, for the mantra of Haṃsārūḍhā Vāgīśvarī:
*Oṃ*, the Seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śakti, the Metre (*chandaḥ*) is the Goddess Gāyatrī, and the Deity is Haṃsārūḍhā Vāgīśvarī.
The deity is Vāk; the application is for the *Vājapeya* sacrifice.
Herein is the meditation on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by means of the seed-syllable *Vāgbhava*:
[one should meditate upon] Vāṇī, whose face shines like the full moon, who possesses the luster of camphor and jasmine, and who is marked by the crescent moon.
With her own hands, she respectfully holds the darkness-destroying lute, the cord of liberation, a jar brimming with nectar, and knowledge; she has lofty breasts,
her body is adorned with divine ornaments, and she rides upon a swan.

Having meditated thus, "I worship her who is firmly established," the mantra is as follows: *oṃ hrīṃ aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ sarasvatyai namaḥ*. Alternatively, the Bālā-mantra is: *oṃ asya śrībālātripurāmantrasya dakṣiṇāmūrtiṛṣiḥ gāyatrīcchandaḥ*.

The meters are the three *chandases*; the deity is the goddess Tripurā; the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *Aiṃ*; the power (*śakti*) is *Klīṃ*; the pin (*kīlaka*) is *Sauṃ*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining my mantra during recitation. By reciting the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) twice, the six limbs [are consecrated].

She whose limbs are adorned with earrings shining like pearls of meditation, who possesses necklaces, strings of pearls, and finger-rings, whose lotus-feet are radiant with golden anklets and tinkling bells, and who wears a supreme crest-jewel of rubies.
She bears the moon, the sun, and the blue lotus;

she holds in her right hands the noose, the goad, the book, and the rosary; she resembles the full moon invoked by the rising [light] from the right; she has a gracious countenance and is radiant with three eyes.

The wise should meditate upon the Goddess Bhagavatī, who has risen from the *mūlādhāra* into the heart-lotus; she whose limbs are radiant with milk-white luster, who possesses the sound of garlands and unguents,
and who is seated within the *nṛāsa* (lotus) bud amidst solitary flowers.
HAYENMEDVALE AIṂ KLĪṂ SAUḤ— thus is the mantra.
This concludes the section on Durgā from the *Ajñānadhvāntadīpikā*, composed by Somanātha, son of Mahā-mohopādhyāya Maheśanātha Bhaṭṭa.

The Fourth Chapter, titled "The Discourse on Mantras. Now, the illustrious mantra: Oṃ. Of this illustrious Ekākṣara-mantra, Bhārgava is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), the one-syllabled Śrī is the deity (devatā), and Śaṃvī is the seed-syllable (bīja).

"Jaṃ" is the *svāhā*-power and "raṃ" is the *kīlaka*; the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining great wealth. One should perform the six-limbed ritual assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the seed-syllables endowed with the six long vowels.
As for the meditation (*dhyāna*): may there be [the Goddess] who possesses many feet, and who grants protection and the boon of granting desires.

Padmā, who possesses a pair of arms white with the luster of the moon, holding a jar filled with water from the hand of the Creator, adorned with a multitude of jewels, a most pure silken garment, garlands, and ointments— may she protect you.

Having meditated thus: "The lotus, Nābhi, the chest, the arm, the thigh, the knee, the foot, the lotus, the serpent, and Śrī are resorted [to]," one who has been initiated and has conquered the senses should mutter the mantra *Śrīṃ* one hundred thousand times; he should offer oblations ten thousand times.

One should offer oblations there with lotuses drenched in honey, or with sesame seeds drenched in honey, or with bilva fruits—either individually or three together—for the sake of the best of practitioners. Now follows the mantra for Karaṇavāsinī: *namaḥ*.
*Svāhā* to the one dwelling in the lotus (*Kamalavāsinī*). Of this mantra of the illustrious Kamalavāsinī, Dakṣa Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chandas*),
Kamalavāsinī is the deity (*devatā*), *Raṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *Svāhā* is the power (*śakti*).

The application (*viniyoga*) for the recitation (*japa*) of the *naṃkīlaka* mantra for the purpose of attaining wealth is as follows: *oṃ devyai hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ panyai śirase svāhā*; *oṃ viṣṇupatnyai namaḥ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*;
*oṃ varadāyai kavacāya huṃ*; [to her] who possesses all forms...
Maḥ, to the Eye; Oṃ, salutation to Her who dwells in the lotus. Phaṭ, to the Weapon. The visualization:
Seated upon a lotus, with lotus-like eyes, she holds a pair of lotuses and the gestures of granting boons (*vara*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
Her divine body is radiant with these splendors.

May the illustrious Goddess Bhavānī grant you prosperity— she who illuminates the three worlds, who is the sustenance for liberation, whose jar-like breasts are beautiful with pearl necklaces, and who wears jeweled anklets, waist-bands, necklaces, armlets, and a crown.

One should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) of one million recitations with lotuses smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), followed by oblations and other rites at one-tenth that number. Now follows the heart-mantra of Mahālakṣmī:
Mahālakṣmī is the deity; *Śrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*); *Hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*).
*Klīṃ* is the *kīlaka*. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining *Lakṣmī* during recitation (*japa*).

*Oṃ oṃ śrīṃ prasīda hṛdayāya namaḥ* (Oṃ Oṃ Śrīṃ, be gracious; salutation to the heart). *Oṃ hrīṃ prasīda śirase svāhā* (Oṃ Hrīṃ, be gracious; svāhā to the head). *Klīṃ prasīda śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (Klīṃ, be gracious; vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock). *Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ prasīda kavacāya huṃ* (Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, be gracious; huṃ to the armor).

*Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*, obeisance to the three gracious eyes; *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ prasīda mahālakṣmi astrāya phaṭ*. The visualization (*dhyāna*): [She who holds] in Her hands a pair of lotuses, a vessel, and a mirror, with shimmering necklaces, armlets, and bracelets.
May the Goddess— adorned with a great crown and armlets, her earrings shimmering, seated upon a lotus,
surrounded by female attendants, clad in white unguents and silken garments, worshipped by divine hosts, and the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence— be meditated upon within me.

One should recite the mantra: *Śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kamalālaye prasīda mahālakṣmi namaḥ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*. For this auspicious mantra, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations, followed by offerings of bilva leaves or fruits numbering one-tenth of that amount.
The *homa* [is performed] with offerings smeared with the three sweets (*madhuratriya*). Now follows the *Hṛdayalakṣmī-mantra*:

For this *Śrī-hṛdayalakṣmī-mantra*, Brahmā is the *ṛṣi*, Gāyatrī is the *chandas*, and the goddess Lakṣmī dwelling in the heart is the *devatā*. [It is used] for recitation (*japa*) for the purpose of pleasing Lakṣmī.
The ritual application (*niyoga*): *Oṃ aiṃ* for the heart; *Oṃ hrīṃ* for the head; *Oṃ śrīṃ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*);

*Oṃ klīṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*); *Oṃ sauḥ* for the eyes; *Oṃ jagatprasūtyai namaḥ* for the weapon (*astra*). The visualization (*dhyāna*): [She] has the luster of the rising sun and is adorned with a crescent moon.
She who shines with the moon atop her six crests, adorned with ornaments of gems and jewels,
holding rays formed of mani-stones, bearing within her hands a lotus and the Kaustubha gem set in their midst, she who possesses a beautiful smile and eyes like lovely lotuses.
One should meditate on the Supreme Goddess as being endowed with the three *natras*. Having thus meditated, the mantra is:
*Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sauṃ jagatprasūtyai namaḥ*. The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this consists of ten hundred thousand recitations, [offered] with ghee, lotuses, and *bilva* flowers.
Having led [the breath] for one hundred and eight times while standing in water reaching up to the neck,
