and having meditated upon the Goddess in the sun with arms extended as far as the eyes, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; thus one immediately obtains health and acquires wealth.
One should constantly offer oblations of fried rice (*chita*) one thousand and eight times;

before long, prosperity (*lakṣmī*) will certainly arise. Now follows the mantra that bestows the four aims of life (*caturvarga*): for this glorious mantra, Bhṛgu is the seer (*ṛṣi*) and Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chaṃdas*).
The seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *Śrīṃ*, the deity is the Goddess who bestows the four aims of life (*caturvarga*), the power (*śakti*) is *Īṃ*, and the pin (*kīlaka*) is *Raṃ*.

This is the application (*viniyoga*) for recitation (*japa*) for the purpose of attaining great wealth. One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the six long vowels. As for the meditation (*dhyāna*): [She is] like a ruby...
She is being constantly sprinkled by four lofty elephants, resembling the brilliance of the sun and moon,

whose trunks are immersed in the water of jeweled jars; she holds in her lotus-like hands the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and the pair of lotuses and fearlessness (*abhaya*), while her eyes long for the beloved of Hari.
Having meditated thus upon the Goddess seated on a lotus, with a *parijāta* creeper as her upper garment, one should then perform the *puraścaraṇa* of the Tripuṭā-Lakṣmī mantra:
*aiṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*. The preliminary rite consists of twelve hundred thousand recitations, followed by ten thousand oblations (*homa*) of red lotuses mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
Having performed *prāṇāyāma* with the root mantra, and having first [assigned] the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs], [one recites]:

*oṃ śrīṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, *hrīṃ śirase svāhā*, *klīṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*, *śrīṃ kavacāya huṃ*, *hrīṃ netrebhyo vauṣaṭ*, *klīṃ astrāya phaṭ*. Then, the meditation (*dhyāna*): [He is] shining like ninefold gold...

Having meditated thus— [on the Lord] seated upon the shoulders of lotuses placed on ever-newly increased lion-thrones, whose bodies are like the Kalpa-trees, and who wear jeweled crowns set with rubies— one should perform the preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa*) of twelve hundred thousand times for the mantra *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ*.
A sacrifice (*homa*) should be performed with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from the *bilva* tree, ten times the number of the [previous] oblation, soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhura*).
Thus ends the *Yāmajñānadhvāntadīpikā*, composed by Somanātha, son of the great preceptor Śrī Maheśabhaṭṭa.
The fifth chapter, titled "The Section on the Lakṣmī Mantra," from the *Pikā*.
Now begins the section on the Viṣṇu mantras: Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī-Vāsudeva.

Śrī Oṃ namo viṣṇave surapataye mahābalāya svāhā. Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya. This is the Anuṣṭubh mantra. [Salutation] to the one whose form consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, whose activity is the ornamentation of the Vedas, the Puruṣa of the Praṇava and Udgītha, the Great One.
And [the salutation] to the head: *namaḥ*. Now, the six-syllabled mantra of Śrī Rāma:

for this Śrī Rāma-ṣaḍakṣara-mantra, Agastya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Paṅkti is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śrī Rāmacandra is the deity (*devatā*), *rāṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and it is for the attainment of the fourfold aims of human life (*caturvidhapuruṣārtha*).

The application for the purpose of accomplishment is in recitation; one should perform the placement of the limbs using the seed-syllable endowed with the six long vowels. Now, as for the meditation: [He is] dark like the petal of a blue lotus, adorned with a crown of matted locks, and on his left side is a bull.
The Supreme Goddess Sītā, whose nature is the womb of all things, fair as a *caṃpaka* flower,
adorned with white garments and divine ornaments, possessing two arms and jeweled earrings— [the two gods] hold a bow and arrows [and gaze upon] Sītā.
One should meditate thus: "One should remember her as having lotus-like hands," and then recite the mantra: *RĀM Rāmāya namaḥ*.

Having performed the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) of one hundred thousand recitations of the syllables, one should offer oblations into the fire with *aśoka* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), consisting of ten parts of that [recitation], O Sage.
For the sake of attainment, this Śrī Rāma mantra consists of six syllables;
as it is stated in the Tāpinī: "The six-syllabled mantra of one's own desire-power (kāma-śakti), consisting of the six long vowels, bestows the four aims of life; [it is] Brahmā Sammohana."

Śaktidakṣiṇāmūrti is said [to be the deity]; O Sage, Śiva is declared here to be the brother of Agastya according to this sequence. Alternatively, the sage is Viśvāmitra, beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma; and the meter is known as Gāyatrī of Manu.

The meditation, worship, and all other rites for the deity Śrī Rāmacandra have been proclaimed as before. For this Śrī Rāma-Ṣaḍakṣara-mantra, Brahmā is the Ṛṣi, Gāyatrī is the Chandas, Śrī Rāmacandra is the Devatā, *rāṃ* is the Bīja, and *svāhā* is the Śakti.

My *śakti* is for the sake of accomplishing the fourfold goals of human life (*caturvidhapuruṣārtha*). The application is in *japa*, and the mantra consists of only two syllables; one should assign the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) to it.
For meditation: [one should contemplate] him who is dark-complexioned, lotus-eyed, with beautiful hands, seated in the *vīrāsana*.

Behold Rāghava, who is seated upon a throne, wearing yellow garments, holding his own knees with both arms, and adorned with various ornaments such as a crown and armlets; he gazes upon Sītā, who stands by his side, her hands joined at her chest, resembling a flash of lightning.

I worship the one with radiant limbs; having worshipped [the deity] in the fire, one should offer oblations into the fire with auspicious flowers for one hundred thousand times and for a tenth part of the mantra. Then, one should feed the Brahmins and worship in the Varuṇa-pīṭha, worshipping indeed with the root-mantra.
This is the procedure for the six-syllable mantra of Rāma: *oṃ rāmāya sītāvallabhāya svāhā*;
this is the ten-syllable mantra. *oṃ daśānanavināśanāya svāhā*;
this is the thirteen-syllable mantra, [addressed to] the Destroyer of the Ten-faced One (*Daśāsya*).

"Protect me! Grant me life! Grant me prosperity! Grant me all [the fruits], such as the state of a seer (*ṛṣi*), and so forth, as before. Thus ends the Rāma-mantra in its entirety: *oṃ klīṃ hṛṣīkeśāya namaḥ | śrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ śrīṃ dharāya trailokyamohanāya namaḥ*.

Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One in the form of the Primeval Boar; salutations! O Lord of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, grant me the sovereignty of the earth, bestow it upon me, svāhā! Thus ends the mantra of Varāha.
Oṃ lauṃ, to the Blessed Goddess Earth, O Upholder of the Earth, svāhā! Thus [ends the mantra] of Pṛthivī.
The mantra *Hūṃ* is also the Varāha-mantra. Next is the Gopāla-mantra:
the single-syllable *Klīṃ*; the ten-syllable mantra is *Gopījanavallabhāya svāhā*; and *Oṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya gopī...*.

Svāhā to the Beloved of the People! Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ, Svāhā to the Beloved of the Cowherds! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ, Svāhā to Kṛṣṇa, Govinda, the Beloved of the Gopīs! Aiṃ Klīṃ, [Svāhā] to Kṛṣṇa, Hrīṃ Govinda...
Dāya-Śrī-Gopījana-Vallabhāya Svāhā! Sauṃ Aiṃ Klīṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Gopījana-Vallabhāya Svāhā! Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya Svāhā! Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya Govindāya Svāhā!
Oṃ namo bhagavate rukmiṇīvallabhāya svāhā | Hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ gopījanavallabhāya svāhā | Namaḥ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | "Kṛṣṇaḥ" is the two-syllabled [mantra].
*Klīṃ Kṛṣṇaḥ* is three syllables; *Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya* is four syllables;
*Kṛṣṇāya Namaḥ* is five syllables; *Klīṃ Kṛṣṇāya Namaḥ* is six syllables;
*Kṛṣṇāya Klīṃ Klīṃ* is five syllables; and *Gopāya* is two syllables.
*gopālāya svāhā*—six syllables; *śrīkṛṣṇāya svāhā*—six syllables; *kṛṣṇāya govindāya*—seven syllables; *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya govindāya*—eight syllables; *klīṃ kṛṣṇāya govindāya klīṃ*.
The nine-syllable mantra: *dadhibhakṣaṇāya svāhā*. The eight-syllable mantra: *suprasannātmane namaḥ*. The eight-syllable mantra: *śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya klīṃ*.
The seven-syllable mantra: *klīṃ laṃ klīṃ śyāmāṅgāya namaḥ*. This...
The ten-syllable mantra: *vālavapuṣe kṛṣṇāya svāhā*. The ten-syllable mantra:
*śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ kṛṣṇāya klīṃ*. The seven-syllable mantra:
*vālavapuṣe klīṃ kṛṣṇāya svāhā*. *Kṛṣṇāya klīṃ klīṃ klīṃ kṛ...*
To Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the sound of the flute; to the crest-jewel (Cūḍāmaṇi); *klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*;
to Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Śrīṃ Bhrāṃ Jrīṃ Bhīṃ, the conqueror; to Kṛṣṇa, who is eternally intent on play, whose mind is liberated, and who is fond of dancing; to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; *klīṃ* go.
*pījanavalabhāya svāhā*. This is the *mālā-mantra*: *śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ oṃ klīṃ śrīṃ matantavapuṣottama apratimarūpa lakṣmīnivāsa sakalakṣobhaṇa sarvastrīhṛdayavidāraṇa...*

Japa (2) dīpaya (2) śoṣaya (2) māraya (2) staṃbhaya (2) mohaya (2) drāvaya (2) ākarṣaya (2) the minds of the beautiful women of gods and humans who cause great intoxication on the battlefield; [subdue] all!
O you who possess the supreme excellence that creates all splendor, O granter of all desires,
[protect] such-and-such with the Sudarśana discus, the Kaumodakī mace, the Nandaka sword, the Śārṅga bow and arrows, and the noose.
Bind! (2) Crunch! Strike with the *kuśa* grass! (2) Go! (2) O Śrī Kiṃtiṣṭha! Why do you neglect this? May all that is desired quickly be accomplished!
*klīṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Of this [mantra] of the glorious Gopāla Śrīkṛ...
For the *Ṣoḍaśanāmamālā-mantra*, Nārada is the seer (*ṛṣi*);

Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Gāyatrī is the meter; the unmanifest primordial nature (*avyaktaprakṛti*) is the presiding deity (*adhiṣṭhātrī*) Śrī Durgā, and the deity (*devatā*) is Śrī Gopāla; *klīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*vīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and it is for my righteousness (*dharma*).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of liberation from bondage: *Oṃ namaḥ kṛṣṇāya goviṃdāya devakīputrāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. *Oṃ klīṃ glauṃ klīṃ namo bhagavate nandaputrāya bālavapuṣe śyāma...*

*Oṃ malāgāyagopījanavallabhāya svāhā*. *Oṃ nandanandanāya svāhā*. *Oṃ nandini nandana-pradāya naṃ me dehi deva svāhā*. The ritual assignment (*nyāsa*): *Oṃ klīṃ* to the heart; *Oṃ kṛṣṇāya* to the head.

*Goviṃdāya śikhā*, *oṃ gopījana-kavaca*, *vallabhāya netra*, *svāhā astre*. One should meditate upon Govinda, the lotus-eyed one, who is composed of mind, enchanting the world, and beautiful as the Vṛndāvana forest.
By the thousands, she was like a cluster of lotuses; her eyes were like bees sent from the lotus-face of her own self; she was tormented by the arrows of Kama and desired an embrace for a moment;
and her pearl necklace shone like a school of fish upon its high breast.

With their bosoms heaving as they bowed, their lower garments slipping down, and their minds faltering at the sound of their own names being called, they captivated [the hearts of men] with various amorous gestures and haughty expressions,
bearing faces that possessed the luster of blooming blue lotuses.

I bow to Govinda, whose body is adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark and the noble Kaustubha gem, who is fond of garlands, clad in yellow garments, and most beautiful; whose form is worshipped by the lotus-eyes of the gopīs, who is surrounded by hosts of cows and cowherds, and whose divine limbs are intent on playing the flute.

Then, after meditation, I worshiped Bhūṣaṇa in Dvāravatī, which was surrounded by excellent palaces possessing the splendor of a thousand suns, by numerous wish-fulfilling trees, and by jeweled pavilions with pillars, archways,
and porticos made of blazing gems and jewels. In that place of blooming flowers...
In the center were two ponds adorned with guggulu resin, citra-flowers, and canopies, strewn with pearls and lotus-precious stones, and featuring streams of royal gems;
beneath a celestial tree from which a stream of jewels flowed incessantly, they shone like rows of jewel-lamps.
Possessing a splendor equal to ten million moons, suns, and lightning flashes, beautiful in every limb, gentle,
and adorned with all ornaments; clad in yellow garments, with hands radiant with the discus, conch, mace, and lotus, and incessantly shedding streams of jewels from his plow.
Touching the water-pot with his left foot, he should place the two pots upon his shoulder;
with the power (śakti) of the directions, beginning with Ajitī and Sundarī,
he should place those two pots with his right and left hands, [bestowing] jewels upon Mitra, Vṛnda, and Sulakṣmaṇa.

Having extracted the earth, two jars filled with jewels were placed by them; Jāmbavatī and Suśīlā were on the left and right respectively. Outside, sixteen thousand beloveds surrounded him in number; one should meditate upon [him] as golden.
Then, the hosts of their maidservants, radiant with the splendor of the Ratnauca-dhārā-yu-kula,
stood there in countless numbers; and beyond that, the eight Siddhis and then the nine Niyatis filled the entire earth as far as it extends.

The limit [of the lineage] is Tiddhāraka; outside of that are all the Vṛṣṇis, as well as the Asuras and others, as before. Thus, one should perform the worship of the Ṛṣis and so forth, the meditation, and the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) for the mantras of Gopāla. Now, the mantra of Nṛsiṃha: *hrīṃ ugraṃ vīraṃ mahāviṣṇum*.

I bow to the blazing Nṛsiṃha, whose faces are turned in all directions, the terrifying yet auspicious one, the death of death; *hrīṃ oṃ kṣauṃ*. Now follows the Hayagrīva mantra: *oṃ udgīrat praṇavodgītha sarvavāgīśvareśvaraḥ sarvadevamaya*.

*ttyasarvabodheya bodhaya svāhā*. Now, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*): *oṃ udgīraḥ* for the heart; *praṇavodgīthaḥ* for the head; *sarvavāgīśvaraḥ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *sarvadevamayāścitya* for the armor (*kavaca*); *sarvaṃ bodhaya* for the two eyes (*netra*); [and *svāhā* for the weapon (*astra*)].

Svāhā! For this *astra* mantra, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of thirty-three hundred thousand recitations. An oblation (*homa*) should be performed with jasmine flowers (*kundapuṣpa*) soaked in the three sweets (*trimadhu*), using one-tenth of that number. The *Nṛsiṃha* mantra is: *Āṃ hrīṃ kṣauṃ krauṃ huṃ phaṭ*.

For this mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), the Paṅkti is the meter (chandaḥ), and Nṛsiṃha is the deity (devatā). One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) using the very syllables of the root mantra.
As for the meditation (dhyāna): [one should contemplate Him] with a trembling tongue due to anger and His own mouth wide open.

She whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire; whose radiance, red from the feet upward, is white above; who has pierced the body of the lord of the Daityas; who holds a conch, discus, noose, goad, thunderbolt, mace, and sword; and who possesses sharp-pointed fangs—[I bow to her] adorned with jewels.

One should know that for this mantra, which praises Nṛsiṃha who is beyond all conceptualization, there are six hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), and the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites should be performed with milk-rice mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) at one-tenth the number of recitations.
Now follows the Garuḍa mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate garuḍāya kālā...*
O you of dark complexion, come, come! O you whose tongue is the fire of time, cause to fall! (2) Delude! (2) Disperse! (2) Cause to wander! (2) Strike! (2) Blow! (2) Cook!
(2) Churn! HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ! Previously born from the midst of the milk ocean...

Having meditated upon that lotus, which consists of the letters of the alphabet and is of the nature of nectar, one should recollect the eight fangs on the eight petals of that lotus; and at the top of those fangs, one should place the four nectar-seeds—*va*, *ka*, *haṃ*, and *vaṃ*—in the mouth, heart, navel, and secret organ respectively. This is the Śrī-vitattva.

Having meditated upon Garuḍa— who is not bitten by one who has not so intended— possessing the color of a moonstone (candrakānta) above his head, consisting of his own radiance, and flooding the fangs with a stream of nectar issuing from a conch filled with nectar situated at his chest,
one should recite the mantra while performing this meditation.
If one who has been bitten by a snake merely meditates thus, he shall rise up free from poison and live for a long time.
*Oṃ namo bhagavate garuḍāya pakṣirājāya harivāhanāya vinatāgarbharatnāya kaśyapātmajāya*.

O you who have the form of the great Indra who carries the nectar, O you who are the crest of the mountain, O you whose form is the ultimate cause, O you of immeasurable strength and prowess: withdraw the poison! Release it! Move it! Cast it down! Render it poisonless! Even poison shall become nectar.
"Obeisance to the one whose form is like the glorious food, svāhā! Obeisance to Nala, Varu, Kṣiya, svāhā!
By this mantra of Garuḍa, even poison that has been consumed becomes nectar when consecrated by Garuḍa. Thus [ends] the section on Garuḍa.

The *Ḍamantra*. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Vaiṣṇava Mantras," in the *Majñānadhvāntadīpikā* composed by Śrī Somanātha, son of the venerable Mahopādhyāya Śrī Maheśabhaṭṭa. Now, the [seventh]...

The brief description [of the mantra] is as follows: *tāra* (oṃ), *ghṛṇi*, *bhṛguḥ* (ṅaḥ) at the end, adorned with the left ear (*vāmakaṇa*) [the letter *sa*], seated on fire (*vahni*), the great *śeṣa* (anusvāra), with two eyes (*netra*), and ending with water (*tya*). This eight-syllabled mantra of the Sun is proclaimed by Amitatejas.
Jasaḥ oṃ ghṛṇi sūrya āditya iti hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ is the three-syllabled mantra;
oṃ hīṃ saṃ haṃsaḥ sūryā ādi haṃsaḥ. Of this Śrī Sūrya-mantra, Devabhārgava is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and Āditya is the deity (devatā).

Oṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Hrīṃ is the power (*śakti*), and Saḥ is the pin (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of pacifying all diseases during the recitation (*japa*). Now, the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): Oṃ *brahmaṇastejo jvalāmaṇe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*—to the heart (0). Oṃ *brahmaṇastejo...* [continues].

Jvālāmaṇi hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—[for] the head (śiras). Oṃ viṣṇu-tejo jvālāmaṇi hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—[for] the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ rudra-tejo jvālāmaṇi hūṃ phaṭ svāhā—[for] the eyes (netra). Oṃ sarva-tejo jvālā... [for] the armor (kavaca).
*Lāmaṇehuṃphaṭ svāhā*—this is the *astra*. Now, the placement of the syllables (*varṇanyāsa*):
*Oṃ namaḥ* on the head; *Oṃ namaḥ ghṛ huṃ phaṭ svāhā* in the mouth; *Oṃ ṇiṃ namaḥ* on the throat; *Oṃ sūṃ namaḥ* in the heart; *Oṃ ryaṃ namaḥ* in the belly; *Oṃ*... [in the feet].
AṂ namaḥ at the navel; OṂ CIṂ namaḥ at the genitals; OṂ TYAṂ namaḥ at the feet.

Meditation: [One should meditate on the Lord] whose hands hold a pair of red lotuses and bestow fearlessness, who is adorned with bracelets, armlets, and earrings, who wears a ruby crown, and who is compassionate toward the wretched.
One should worship the Sun, who possesses the brilliance of the bandhūka flower and has three eyes, while reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times.
With self-control, one should offer one thousand oblations of fuel sticks from milky trees smeared with milk. This is the Sūrya-mantra.
Regarding this *Śrīprāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra* from the *Thaprakīrṇa*:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (*ṛṣi*); the *Ṛg*, *Yajuṣ*, *Sāman*, and *Atharvaṇa* are the meters (*chandas*); and the Consciousness-form Prāṇa-śakti is the deity (*devatā*).
The application (*viniyoga*) for the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for the sake of accomplishing such-and-such a task.

Now, the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): Oṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ (to the heart). Oṃ īṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ śirase svāhā (to the head). Oṃ uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ ūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ (to the crest-lock).

Khā (0) Oṃ eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ, [this is] the armor (kavaca). Oṃ āṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ auṃ, [this is] the three eyes (netratraya). Oṃ āṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ āḥ, [this is] the weapon (astra).
Oṃ yaṃ, O you whose nature is the syllable *ya*, O self of the skin, O self of the marrow!
Oṃ, salutations to the one whose nature is the syllable *saṃ*, the essence of semen (*śukra*);

salutations to the one whose nature is the syllable *haṃ*, the essence of the seed-syllable (*bīja*); Oṃ, salutations to the one whose nature is the syllable *laṃ*, the essence of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); *kṣaḥ*, [salutations to the one whose nature is] the syllable *kṣa*.
Salutations to the embodied Supreme Self. Now, the mantra for the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*):
Śrī. Oṃ Āṃ Hrīṃ Krauṃ Yaṃ Raṃ Laṃ Śaṃ Ṣaṃ Saṃ Haṃ Laṃ Kṣaṃ Haṃsaḥ So’ham Amu...

Whose life-breaths are these life-breaths? Oṃ! (16) The life of so-and-so is established here. Oṃ! (16) The skin, eyes, ears, taste, nose, tongue, smell, speech, hands, feet, and the earth, water, fire, and wind of so-and-so [are here].

"O you whose essence consists of air, ether, sound, touch, form, taste, smell, speech, giving, movement, excretion, and bliss— come here and remain for a long time in my mouth, svāhā! This is the mantra for the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).

Now, for the mantra consisting of the five *lavaṇas* (salts): Aṅgiras is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), Agni, Rātri, Durgā, and Bhadrakālī are the deities (*devatās*), the consonants are the seeds (*vījas*), and the vowels are the powers (*śaktis*). [The recitation count is] one hundred thousand times five.
The application of *kajapa*: salt indeed is exceedingly sharp;
when those two perfected ones are heated with salt, they burn; the five salts cut and pierce; when the salt is being offered into the fire, where [is it not present]?

Delighting in the destruction of living beings, he burns the flesh, skin, bones, and hair of the mouth of the one who recites the *gāyatrī*; with his bones and marrow, he burns the *bhajjikās* for a hundred *yojanas* and for hundreds of days.
In this world, which is like a boat tossed upon an ocean crowded with hundreds of serpents of conceptual construction,
you have crossed over by the power of your ascetic heat; yet, O Lord, even though you have cast off the body,
you are as if pierced by a spear-point and placed upon it.

O Rātrisāti, O Night, O Great Midnight! Having brought him who dwells therein under your own control, quickly bring [the person named] so-and-so under my control. Oṃ hrīṃ ciṭi ciṭi cāṃ muḍālini, bring so-and-so under my control.

"SVĀHĀ" (2)—this is the method for the six limbs. For the rites of killing (*māraṇa*) and driving away (*uccāṭana*), one should append the words "HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. As for the visualization (*dhyāna*): [he is] seated upon a red lotus, possessing the Śakti [consort], and endowed with the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).

O Rāṃ! You who possess immeasurable radiance, whose lofty and pervasive splendor is the refuge for the weary, you who burn away the threefold afflictions; O wielder of the goad, you who have dispelled the heavy burden of her body—her garments and hair being exceedingly dark blue.

Obeisance to the Goddess who eternally protects from worldly existence, whose lotus-like hands shine with the noose, trident, skull-topped staff, and discus, and whose crown is illuminated by the radiance of the conch, sword, trident, and mace.

The goddess whose limbs are inscribed by the Three-Eyed One, who is worshipped by Indra and the other gods, who possesses a face resembling the moon, who has three eyes, who is radiant with a fierce, white fang,
and who holds a skull-cup supreme with auspicious marks.
May Bhadrakālī— resplendent with the sound of a thousand lattices of *ḍamaru*, *śakti*, and tridents,
and radiant with a beautiful garland of tinkling bells—
grant you the attainment of all perfections for a long time. This mantra should be recited ten thousand times (*ayuta*).

Regarding the preliminary ritual (*puraścaraṇa*) for the recitation (*japa*): for the initial recitation of a thousand [mantras], the preliminary ritual consists of ten thousand recitations; an oblation (*havana*) of clarified butter (*ājya*) must be performed at one-fourteenth of that number. Starting from the eighth lunar day until the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), this should be done every night.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations, or a thousand, with powder measured by a *kuṇḍava* and combined with honey and clarified butter.
By performing such homas for seven nights, the target becomes instantly subdued through the homa; he becomes submissive and subject to one's will. This is the ritual application (*prayoga*).

In the place of "Kāle" in the mantra, one should join the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) where it does not belong and perform the oblation; this is the mantra as stated in the *Devaprakāśikā*.
Two *karṣas* are said to be [the weight of] oyster shells, and four *karṣas* are said to be [the weight of] *laca*.
A kuṇḍa twice the size of a *prasṛti* is prescribed for the oblation (*homa*) in rites of pacification (*śāntika*).
Milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, sesame, *garī*, dates, grapes, *vadāma*, and *sarī*— these are used in auspicious rites.

In rites of terrible action (*ghorakarman*), one should summon those whose desires have not fallen away; for rites such as killing with turmeric, salt, yellow arsenic (*haritāla*), mallets, and so forth, as well as with *dāla*, white mustard, and the like, these substances should be combined together.

One should perform the oblation for the rite; this is the application of the *itilaba* ritual. Alternatively, for the mantra of releasing prisoners (*vandīmokṣaṇa*), Śukra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and the goddess Śrī-Vandīmokṣaṇī is the deity (*devatā*) for the purpose of loosening iron fetters.

The application (*viniyoga*): One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) using the *māyāvīja* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*) which possesses the six long vowels. The mantra is: *hrīṃ himācale kumārike svāhā*. One should recite this mantra one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times, for each limb. This...

One should recite it every day; then, having written the mantra upon a leaf in this manner and standing upon the root [of the plant], one should perform the recitation one thousand and eight or one hundred times.
That leaf-cake belongs to the man who stands as a captive.

One should release the prisoner for the sake of providing food; then, from the house of the *ākāra*, the release of the prisoner (*vandīmokṣa*) occurs. Thereafter, the householder, according to his own capacity, should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*guru*). Thus ends the ritual procedure for the mantra of releasing prisoners.

The mantra of Thamātaṅgī: *Oṃ ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī sammukhe devi mahāpiśācini hrīṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*. This is the twenty-two syllable mantra. [It is dedicated to] Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālī Mātaṅgī, who brings all under control.
*Karīnamaḥ svāhā*— this consists of nineteen syllables. *Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ he jyeṣṭhamātangi namāmi ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālini trailokyavaśyaṃkari hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Thus, these three *mātaṅgī* mantras consist of thirty-two syllables each;
their meter is the *uttuṃkṛtigāyatrī*,
their deity is the one who bestows swift results, their seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *aiṃ hrīṃ*, and their power (*śakti*) is *svāhā*.

*Śrīṃ klīṃ sauṃ* is the *kīlaka*. For the sake of attaining all desired objects, this is the application (*viniyoga*) for the recitation (*japa*). Now, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*): *Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī* is the heart (*hṛdaya*), *Samukhī* is the head (*śiras*), *Devī* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*), [and] *Mahā*... [is the armor (*kavaca*)].
*Piśācinī-kavaca*: Hrīṃ-netra-tra-ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ-astra. Now the second [mantra]: Ucchiṣṭa-hṛdaya, Caṇḍālī-śiraḥ svāhā, Mātaṅgī-śikhā, Sarvavaśaṃkarī-kavaca. Na.
Maḥ-netra Svāhā; Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Klīṃ Sauṃ—Astra; He Jyeṣṭhamātangi—Hṛdaya; Namāmi—Śiras; Uchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī—Kavaca; Trailokyavaśaṅkarī—Netra.

In this regard, the mantra is *tatra hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is as follows: one should meditate upon the Goddess, sixteen years of age, who has attained the state of a corpse, who is reeling from the intoxication of honey-liquor, who is dark-complexioned, clad in crimson garments, possessing full breasts, and adorned with a necklace of *guñjā* berries.
One should meditate upon the divine Mātaṅgī, the Uchiṣṭacāṇḍālinī, who is as dark as fresh collyrium, holding in her two hands a stainless skull-cup and a sharp knife, within the lotus of one's mind.

With feet moistened by water, her garments radiant with beauty, her hands shining with sharp luster, her breasts slightly bent, wearing pearls and coral, bearing earrings of black antelope skin and white conch, and possessing lips like the bimba fruit and a beautiful smile; Kṛṣṇā... [smiling].
Having meditated upon her— who has a braid with scattered curls, lotus-like eyes, and is dark as a young parrot— one should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) one hundred thousand times;
and with a tenth part of that, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) and other rites using curds, white mustard seeds, and rice grains.
Now, the *siddhi-mantra* of the Great Goddess (*Mahādevī*) of Cambodia is written here as it is:
*Oṃ*. Of this *śrī-mahādevī-mantra*, Kauśika Viśvāmitra is the *ṛṣi*, *anuṣṭubh* is the *chandas*, and the deity is the illustrious Mahādevī.

*Tāṃ* is the seed-syllable; *svāhā* is for the purpose of accomplishing the task of liberation from the power [of ignorance]. This is the application (*viniyoga*). Now, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*): *oṃ* for the heart, *i* for the head, *ī* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *rauṃ* for the armor (*kavaca*), *ī* for the weapon (*astra*). As for the meditation (*dhyāna*): one should meditate thus... [text ends]
One should worship Guhā— who possesses a mass of peacock feathers, whose lower lip is like a dark coral sprout,
who holds a bow and arrows in her hands, who is clothed in blue garments, and who is magnificent—
with offerings on the eighth lunar day falling on a Tuesday, or on a day when it is a Tuesday alone.

Now the mantra: *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ trailokyamohini me abhīṣṭamanorathaṃ suvraṃ kuru svāhā*. For this mantra, the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one thousand and eight recitations, followed by ten percent of that in offerings of sesame and ghee.

The description of the mantras for the rising of the sun and other [planets], titled "Dināhoma," from the *Majñānadhvāntadīpikā* composed by Śrī Somanātha, son of the venerable Mahopādhyāya Śrī Maheśabhaṭṭa.
The Seventh Illumination (7). Regarding this mantra of the illustrious Gandharva King Viśvāvasu: the seer is Kauśika Viśvāmitra, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and [the deity is] Śrī Viśvāvasu.

The deity is the Gandharva King named Suta; *oṃ* is the seed-syllable, and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). For the sake of attaining my desired maiden, this is the application in recitation (*japa*). The six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): *namo bhagavate* on the thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*).
To the Gandharva King Hṛda (at the heart), to Viśvāvasu at the head of Tarjaśiras; may my desired Śikhā (crown lock) be bent.
Meditating upon meditation, she dwells in the ocean of milk, the best of juices, like sugarcane.
The mantra of that man who, with a pair of eyes fashioned from a garland of white lotuses offered by hosts of maidens, beholds the Lord of the Gandharvas,
Viśvāvasu, with a gracious countenance.
Having meditated upon the desired maiden, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times with this fixed resolve: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the King of Gandharvas, Viśvāvasu!
Grant me the maiden named so-and-so, who is my desire."

Svāhā! Furthermore, regarding this mantra of the illustrious King of the Gandharvas: Kauśika Viśvāmitra is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and the deity is the illustrious Gandharva king named Viśvāvasu.

Oṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Svāhā is the power (*śakti*). For the purpose of attaining my desired maiden, there is the application (*viniyoga*) in recitation (*japa*). The six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): Oṃ to the heart;
Viśvāvasu by name, the Gandharva, to the head; Kanyakā [to the crown].
To the one whose name is the sovereign, for the crest-lock; with a hundred thousand [recitations], for the armor;
to the one whose nature is the head, adorned with ornaments, give this girl named so-and-so; to the one who is the eye, salutations to that Viśva.
VASE SVĀHĀ. For the meditation on Astra:
one should contemplate the Leader of the Gandharvas, who has the form of the sun, whose two breasts hold flowers in his hands, and who wields the bow and the Mohana weapon.

Having meditated upon Viśvāvasu, the lord of the Siddhas, who is praised by songs sung by Gandharva maidens, whose lips are joined with a lute white as a wish-fulfilling flower, and who possesses ornaments as red as red sandalwood paste applied to the mind— I bow to him.

Oṃ! Viśvāvasu by name is the Gandharva, the lord of maidens; to him who is endowed with a hundred thousand [forms], who possesses beautiful form, fine ornaments, and a golden body, I bow—to him, the maiden named so-and-so, grant me.
One should recite this mantra— "Viśvāvasave svāhā"— over water while holding a water-pot seventeen times,
or one hundred and eight times, or one hundred times; by doing so for a month, one obtains a daughter of the Nāgas adorned with ornaments.
The doubt is removed. Thus ends the procedure for obtaining a daughter from the Gandharva King.
Now follows the mantra of Hanumān: For this venerable mantra of Hanumān, Rāmacandra is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), and Śrī Hanumān is [the deity].

The deity is Mahāvīra; the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is the son of the Wind-god (Hanuman); the power (*śakti*) is the son of Añjanī; the *kīlaka* is *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The application (*viniyoga*) for my recitation is for the sake of attaining all desires. [The six long vowels: *ṣaṭ dīrgha*.
One should fashion the six limbs with the seed-syllable *bhājālajjā* and the six-limbed mantra; one should meditate upon the meditation [of him] who is like the rising sun,
who destroys the pride of the enemies of the gods, and whose preeminent fame is praised by the lord of the gods.

One should always meditate upon the god Hanuman, who is blazing with radiance, accompanied by Sugrīva and all the other monkeys, clearly fond of the ultimate truth, and possessing eyes as red as blood; having thus meditated, one should recite: *Oṃ hanumate*.
O Hero of supreme prowess, accomplish all tasks! HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. This is the second mantra. OṂ NAMO BHAGAVATE PRAKAṬAPARĀKRAMĀKRĀNTASAKALADIṄMAṆḌALĀYA YAŚO...
Salutations to the one whose vajra-body makes the three worlds like a mere canopy of flowers;
to the incarnation of Rudra who is ever intent on destroying the wicked; to the burner of the city of Laṅkā; to the one who took delight in leaping across the ocean; to the Ten-faced One.

O you whose body is joined at the neck, who have practiced celibacy from childhood, who possess profound speech, who are the destroyer of ḍākinīs—Oṃ hrīṃ! O Great Ashes! Remove, remove all poison; agitate the enemy forces! (2)
Accomplish all my activities! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Thus ends the Mālā-mantra of Hanumān. Of this Śrī Mālā-mantra, Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas),
Śrī Hanumān is the deity (devatā), *haṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *svāhā* is the power (śakti), and *svāhā* is the pin (kīlaka).
The application (*viniyoga*) for the recitation (*japa*) for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings is as follows: the ritual assignment of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
*Oṃ namo bhagavate añjanīyāya*—to the heart (0). *Rudramūrtaye*—to the head (0). *Vāyuputrāya*—to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) (0). *Añjanī*... [to the armor (*kavaca*)] (0).
*Garbharatnāyakavaca*: Oṃ rāmadūtāya netrāya brahmāstranivāraṇāya svāhā. *Astramantra*. Visualization:
[One should meditate on the deity] as brilliant as a crystal, possessing a radiant luster, two-armed, with palms joined in *añjali*, and adorned with two earrings.

One should perform worship, either in a Vaiṣ� who is like a lion to the lotus-face of Yashas (Lakṣmī), or before Śiva, the delighter of the city of Ayodhyā; indeed, one should perform it upon a Vaiṣṇava or Śaiva pedestal. Then, for the purpose of beholding Hanumān—

The ritual for Rasādha is now described: having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, the twice-born, having performed his daily rites, goes to a river; having bathed there and invoked the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) behind him, he should recite the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) one hundred times and sprinkle [the site] with water.
Having abandoned the previous dwelling by that same count and having donned another dwelling,
one should then perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the bank of the Gaṅgā or on the peak of a mountain:
*āṃ* to the heart, *iśi* to the head, *oṃ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *aiṃ*.

*Kava* is the three eyes (*auṃ-netra-trayā*), *aḥ* is the weapon (*astra*). [This is] the breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Reciting the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and *ka*, one should exhale the air through the left nostril; then, reciting the five groups of consonants (*pañca-varga*).

One should exhale the breath; thus one should perform three rounds of prāṇāyāma. One should perform the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) according to the syllables of the mantra. One should meditate;
one should meditate upon the Lord of Monkeys, accompanied by ten million [monkeys], rushing to conquer Rāvaṇa.

Seeing Lakṣmaṇa, the great hero, whose body was covered in wounds and who had fallen upon the surface of the earth, he conceived a heavy wrath; seizing the mountain that served as his teacher, he made the three worlds tremble with the great sound of his cries of "Alas! Alas! (Hāhākāra).
Having entered up to the realm of Brahmā and assumed a formidable body, one should then recite this mantra:
first uttering the seed-syllable *Śrīṃ*, one should then speak "Pavana" (the Wind), then "Nandana," and then "Devasānena" (by the beloved of Fire). This is the tenth [chapter].

This *Ṛṇoddhāra-mantra* proclaimed by Manu grants the state of the gods to those who practice it; having bestowed great fear for seven days, when only one-third of the night remains, the deity comes at the command of the practitioner.
If the practitioner transcends this illusion (*māyā*), then he attains his desired goal.

He obtains that boon—whether it be knowledge, wealth, or a kingdom that destroys enemies; or else the perfection of his actions, or whatever else is desired by the mind—he attains it at that very moment. This is the truth, the truth; there is no doubt.
Thus ends the *Vīrasana-sādhana* as declared in the *Śrī Hanumat-kalpa*. Now, the mantra of Kālī:
[The seed-syllable] "Kāma" (ka) three times situated in "Vahni" (ra), conjoined with "Rati" (ī) and the "Bindu" (m);
then the pair of "Kūrca" (hūṃ hūṃ), followed by "Lajjā" (hrīṃ) and "Pulana" (kṣrauṃ), then [the word] "Dakṣiṇe" (dakṣiṇe).
One should recite the previous seed-syllables as "Kālike ca iti. Having placed the fire within the bride, it is proclaimed as the Queen of Vidyās:
*krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ dakṣiṇakālike krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*.
"SVĀHĀ"—thus has the extraction of the mantra been stated therein. Now follows the extraction of the single-syllable mantra:
the first letter [Ka] situated in fire [Ra], joined with the thunderbolt [I], the moon [U], and the resonance [M], making "KĪM.
This single-syllable great mantra bestows the fruits of all desires.

This is known as the King of Mantras, difficult to obtain for those of sinful mind, yet easily accessible to devoted practitioners of great soul. The single syllable "Krim" is especially endowed with the three qualities and is the awakener of all scriptures. Krim, Krim.

*Krīṃ*. For these mantras, Bhairava is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Uṣṇik is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī is the deity (*devatā*), *Lajjā* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Kūrca* is the power (*śakti*), and *Khaṃ* is the peg (*kīlaka*). Their application (*viniyoga*) is in recitation for the sake of pleasing the Vidyā.
The six limbs [of worship] are performed with the first seed-syllable joined with the six [consonants]. Now, for the visualization:
she resembles a mass of crushed collyrium, is skillful, resides within a portion of light, has a face with a gentle smile, is gladdened by joy, and is intoxicated with wine. Ā.

She is resplendent with fresh lotus-stalks dripping with blood, glowing with vermilion tilakas made from the hearts and livers of corpses, crimsoned by a garland of fifty severed heads, and adorned with various jewels.
Abounding in excellence, adorned with various ornaments, decorated with bracelets and conch-shell bangles fashioned from human bones, she is mounted upon the chest of a corpse,
licking the breasts of corpses.

She who repeatedly laughs with a hundred morsels of flesh, who brandishes a sword and a severed head in her left hand, bestowing supreme fear; she whose loud roar of "Dantārā Camahārauṃ Drīṃ" is most terrifying, the Śivā of horrific form.

Surrounded by [attendants], she who destroys fear said, "Do not fear, do not fear," to those devoted ones as they uttered terrible cries. When she spoke, saying, "What do you desire? I shall grant it," [she recited] two hundred thousand of their mantras.

For the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, eating sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) during the day while remaining pure, and likewise reciting one hundred thousand times at night while remaining vigilant; thereafter,
the practitioner of the mantra should perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number, offer libations (*tarpaṇa*), and perform the ritual consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
The mantra for the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is as follows:

"Lajjā-bīja, Vadhū-bīja, Kūrca-bīja, and likewise Phaṭ. This five-syllabled vidyā reveals the five elements. As it is stated in the Vārāha-kalpa: "Lajjā-bīja, Vadhū-bīja, and likewise Kūrca-bīja, followed by Phaṭ—this five-syllabled vidyā illuminates the five elements."
"Hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Because she delivers [beings] from saṃsāra, bestows her own self, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, she is celebrated as Ugratārā, the fierce deliverer.
Thus it is stated in the Matsyasūkta: "Oṃ hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ."

Aiṃ Hrīṃ Strīṃ—this is the one-tufted Ekajaṭā; from the great Muktikarī, the Tārā devoid of the weapon-mantra, comes Parṇā Mahānīlasarasvatī; Hrīṃ Strīṃ Hrīṃ—this indeed is the Kullā seed-syllable, Phaṭ is the Śakti.

*Hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *phaṭ* is the power (*śakti*), and *hrīṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of attaining the fruit of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) through recitation (*japa*). Now follows the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*):
*Hrīṃ* to the heart for the embodiment of all supreme speech; *Hrīṃ* to the [head] for the indivisible speech...
HŪṂ for the Brahmā-Agrapīṇyā-Śiras; HRAIṂ for the Viṣṇu-Agrapīṇyā-Kavaca;
HRAUṂ for the Rudra-Agrapīṇyā-Netratraya; HRAḤ for the Sarva-Agrapīṇyā-Astra; Nīlasara.
By Svāti as well, this very Khaṇḍāṅga [is worshipped]: Hrāṃ Ekajaṭāyai for the heart;
Hrīṃ Tāriṇyai for the head; Hūṃ Yajodake for the armor; Hrauṃ Mahāpratisare for the eyes; Hraḥ Pigalograikaṭāyai for the weapon. A...
"Strāyaphaṭ"—thus is the six-limbed mantra of Ekajaṭā. As for the visualization:

she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, is formidable, adorned with a garland of severed heads, is short-statured, has a protruding belly, is terrifying, is clothed in a tiger skin, and possesses the beauty of a young woman.

Endowed with a forest garland, adorned with the moon-disc, four-armed, with a lolling tongue, most terrifying, and bestowing boons; her two right and left hands are joined with a sword and a *kartṛ* knife, and joined with a skull-cup and a blue lotus.

Having meditated upon her as being joined by two left hands, possessing a single tawny and fierce matted lock (ekajaṭā) on her head adorned with Akṣobhya, one should recite [the mantra]. For this, the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations, followed by a tenth part [of that] with offerings of ghee.
One should perform oblations with leaves or fruits of the *bilva* tree; thus ends the section on the Tārā mantra.
Now follows the Mantra of Chinnamastā: I shall describe Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, who bestows the fruit of all desires, by whose mere grace [one attains this].

A man shall become [one with] Sadāśiva; likewise, by reciting ten thousand times the sixteen-syllable mantra beginning with *lakṣmī-lajjā-tathā-māyā*, followed by the twelve measures (*mātrā*), and ending with *vajra-vīrocanyai hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

The sixteen-syllable mantra beginning with *śrīṃ hrīṃ aiṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* is said to bestow the fruits of one's desired objects when recited ten thousand times. *Śrīṃ hrīṃ...* [is the beginning of that mantra].

Aiṃ vajravairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. One who possesses wisdom should recite the mantra beginning with Kāmā, or beginning with Vāg, or beginning with Māyā; or one should recite the Vidyā beginning with Lakṣmī, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life (caturvarga). O Bhairava, this is the mantra of this [Vidyā].

The Seer (Ṛṣi) is Saṃrāj; the Metre (Chandaḥ) is Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā; the Deity (Devatā) is Hrīṃ; the Seed-syllable (Bīja) is Svāhā; the Power (Śakti) is Abhīṣṭasiddhi; the Application (Viniyoga) is for the purpose of success in recitation (Japa). The Six-limbed Assignment (Ṣaḍaṅganyāsa): Āṃ Khaḍgāya Hṛdayāya (Heart); Īṃ Śūlāya Śirase (Head).

*Rase Svāhā*—to the noose (*pāśa*), *Aiṃ*—the armor (*kavaca*). *Aṃ*—to the goad (*aṅkuśa*), *Ne*—the three eyes (*netratraya*). *Aḥ*—to the protection of the vowels (*svarakṣā*), *Astrāṃ*. Regarding meditation (*dhyāna*): one should meditate upon the white lotus of the Mountain-Born (Pārvatī), half-blown, located at one's own navel.

In the center of the womb-maṇḍala, which is adorned with the circle of the source of birth, radiant within its sheath, resembling a hibiscus flower and like the red garment of a bride, and filled with the qualities of passion, existence, delusion, and ignorance— I worship you, the Great Goddess, in that center.
Chinnamastā, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns, who is inseparable from Karālā, who is rushing forward with her own head severed, her terrifying face wide open,
her tongue licking the tips of her fangs, and drinking streams of blood.
He [the minister] constantly meditated upon the Goddess, who wore a garland of bones emerging from her throat,
who had a serpent as her sacred thread,
and who was seated upon a crystal throne.
One should meditate upon Rati and Manobhava standing in reverse union with a sixteen-year-old girl who has full and elevated breasts;
she is joined by Ḍākinī and Varṇinī, positioned on the left and right respectively.

[He meditated upon] the auspicious one, richly adorned with a garland of human heads as her sacred thread, consisting of the splendor of flames, standing in the pratyalīḍha posture, divine, with hair loosened, naked as the directions,
appearing sixteen years of age, and adorned with a necklace of bones. Ḍā...
Kinnī has her left side like the sun and fire at the end of an aeon,
with matted hair like lightning, three eyes, and rows of teeth like a flight of cranes;
she has a face formidable with fangs, full and drooping breasts, and a large belly.
Terrible, with disheveled hair and naked, licking her great tongue,
adorned with a garland of severed heads, holding a skull-cup and a chisel in her left and right hands respectively, she was devouring the mass of flesh from the neck of the Goddess.

The wise should meditate upon that Goddess, who is performing the act of drinking, who is exceedingly terrifying due to the skull held in her hand, and who is attended by the two [messengers] at her feet; for one practicing the preliminary rites (puracaraṇa) of this [mantra], she is at his feet.
The recitation [of the mantra] ten times that amount, as well as the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites, should be understood.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and restraining the senses;
one should offer oblations with flowers or fruits from the palāśa or bilva trees.
Thus ends the mantra of Chinnamastā. Thus [ends] the [work] composed by the illustrious Somanātha, son of the great professor Maheśabhaṭa,
concerning the various phonemes of the mantras of Gandharva, Hanumān, and others.
The Eighth Chapter: Now, the mantra of Bhagalamukhi.
Of this venerable Bhagalamukhi mantra, Narada is the seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is the meter (chandas), and the goddess Śrī Bhagala is the deity; its function is the supreme obstruction of the enemy's army.

The application (*viniyoga*) for the recitation (*japa*) for the sake of accomplishing the task is as follows: *Oṃ hlīḥ* to the heart; *Bagalāmukhī* to the head; *sarvaduṣṭānām* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *vācaṃ mukhaṃ stambhaya* to the armor (*kavaca*); *jihvāṃ kīlakāya* to the eyes; and *atra buddhiṃ nāśaya* to the weapon (*astra*).

*Śaya* (2) *hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ svāhā astrāya phaṭ*. Thus is the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) [mantra]. Some teachers of this mantra say that one should perform the six-limbed ritual using the seed-syllable *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), preceded by the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and possessing the six long vowels. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is upon the tip of the tongue...
I bow to the Goddess who, with her left hand, crushes enemies with the blow of a mace, and with her right hand, is adorned with yellow garments;
having meditated thus, one should recite: *Oṃ hrīṃ bagalāmukhi sarvaduṣṭānāṃ vācaṃ...*
"Paralyze the tongue! Nail it! Destroy the intellect! (2) Oṃ hrīṃ svāhā.

One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with yellow flowers soaked in ghee, using a tenth part of that number as the oblation.
Now, the mantra of Kārtavīryārjuna: Oṃ namo Kārtavīryārjunāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Oṃ namo bhagavate Kārtavīryārjunāya sarvaduṣṭāntakāya tapovalaparāya...

To the crest-jewel of all kings who successively protected the seven continents, whose mind possessed great power, and who lopped off a thousand arms— now follows the *anuṣṭubh* mantra of Kārtavīryārjuna, the king of the Rāma dynasty.
By the mere remembrance of this [mantra], which sustains thousands, that which has been taken away or lost is recovered.
Now, for all these mantras, Dattātreya is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh meter (chanda) is Śrī, and the deity (devatā) is the illustrious Kārtavīryārjuna; may it be for me.
The application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of accomplishing all desired wishes through recitation (japa). As for the visualization (dhyāna):

I bow to the one with a thousand arms, who holds arrows and a bright bow, wears red garments, and possesses a red crown and earrings; he is the destroyer of fear from thieves and other wicked beings, and the granter of desired objects.
To the one who displays great power, Kārtavīrya, this is the *athama* garland-mantra:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate śrīkārtavīryārjunāya haihayanāthāya śrīkārtavīryārjuna sahasrabhuja sarvaduṣṭān...* [The mantra continues].
O you who pierce all with thousands [of weapons], cut [them] with thousands of swords raised by your own hands;
terrify [them] with thousands of roars raised by your own hands; drink [them]; rend them, tear them apart, paralyze them, and hack them to pieces!
Kill! (3) Drive away! Expel! (2) Destroy! (2) Subjugate, subjugate!
(2) Salutation to the beloved of the venerable feet of Dattātreya;
[salutation] to Śrī Kārtavīryārjuna from all sides against those coming from the ocean.
*duḥkhavilaṃṭhakān caurasvamahān maryyāgunmūlaya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. These are the three garland-mantras (*mālāmantra*).
For this mantra, Dattātreya is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) is for the Beloved.
To the Lord of the Earth, [the mantra] *śiraḥ*; to Him who is intent on sporting in the waters of the Revā, *śikhā*;
to the Sovereign of the Haihayas, *kavacaḥ*; *Oṃ sahasrabāhave*, *astraḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) is with one thousand smiling arms, each a staff-like arm.
Did he, with his bow drawn by the breath of his nostrils and fierce arrows like rising suns,
fill the entire universe;
or was it victory itself, adorned with shimmering earrings swaying upon its cheeks?

Having meditated upon Kārtavīryārjuna, one should recite the mantra three thousand times; thereafter, having attained mastery over the mantra, one may accomplish the desired blue rites (nīlakarmāṇi). Thus [ends the section on] Kārtavīryārjuna.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the *namaṃtra*, and then the mantra of Dhūmāvatī: *dāṃ tā var ghī śa vi daṃ tā vī jaṃ dhū mā va tī dva yaṃ*.

This mantra of Dhūmāvatī is declared to be a subduer of enemies. Of this mantra... [pi] (Note: The final fragment "pi" likely indicates the beginning of a further section on the deity's *piṇḍī* or *pīṭha*).
The Ṛṣi is Agastya; the metre is Bṛhatī;
the deity is Dhūmāvatī, who effects the subjugation of speech; the seed-syllable is *dhūṃ*; the power is *svāhā*;
the application is in recitation for the purpose of subjugating enemies. Now, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Dhāṃ dhāṃ to the heart; dhīṃ dhīṃ to the head; dhūṃ dhūṃ to the crest-lock; dhaiṃ dhaiṃ to the armor; dhauṃ dhauṃ to the eyes; dhaṃ dhaḥ to the weapon. The visualization:
She is clad in stainless garments and brings distress to all people.
With her own body rough, her eyes sharp, and her broad hips unadorned,
she was as restless as the sun; her form was distressed by hunger and drenched with perspiration,
and she was always to be meditated upon as Kṛṣṇā, with hair disheveled and a most harsh radiance.

Having meditated thus, the minister Priyakali, naked and eating at night, should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times in a cremation ground and perform an oblation of sesame seeds with a tenth part of that amount. Thus ends the [chapter from the] Śrīmahā...
Thus ends the ninth chapter of the *Jñānadīpikā*, composed by the son of the great preceptor Śrī Maheśabhaṭṭa.
May there be auspiciousness; may it be well for both the scribe and the reader.

Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Kālikā. Oṃ bhrāṃ hrīṃ bhrāḥ!
O Goddess Kālikā, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), summon [the person] named so-and-so! (2 times) Bring her here!
(2 times) Svāhā! Recite ten times at the time of the oblation of clarified butter during the marriage rite.
There is no doubt regarding the month, the flesh, and the meat: Oṃ Cāmuṇḍe,
wielder of the thunderbolt, slayer of the Pralava, hollow-eyed one, you of deformed face, you who laugh with the sound "aṭāṭa," Great Bhairavī, destroyer of all suffering!

O liberator from all bonds, O bringer of fearlessness everywhere, destroy all fevers, svāhā! This mantra should be recited by one who is suffering from fever, or by one afflicted by poison, or by one suffering from indigestion, or by one suffering from abdominal dropsy.

Having written this entire [mantra], which destroys all dust-born [afflictions], upon a leaf of the pippala tree with eight fragrances, one should indeed wear it on the arm; thus those suffering from the three humors and born of dust are cured.
